english.title: Budget session: how MPs examine the finance bill
english.dek: Filing the bill, committee hearings, plenary debate and exchanges with the Senate are all part of the process. We explain how it works using a budget of roughly 4 trillion CFA francs as an example.
keyPoints: The finance bill goes through the Finance Committee, the public session, then the Senate, before its final adoption.
The budget taken for example, of the order of 4,000 billion FCFA, highlights three priorities: school, health and roads.
Citizens can follow public debates, read budget documents and compare voted appropriations to actual spending.

seo.description: From tabling to voting: the course of the finance bill, from the finance committee to the Senate, and what citizens can follow.

body.text: Each year, the budget session places the State budget at the center of the work of the National Assembly. The deputies examine the finance bill, the text which fixes the receipts and expenses for the following financial year. The government prepares it, then drops it off. The examination mobilizes two chambers, the National Assembly then the Senate, and lasts several weeks. To fix the ideas, this article takes the example of a budget of around 4,000 billion FCFA, an order of magnitude given by way of illustration for a country of approximately 2.4 million inhabitants.
A five-step course

items: Filing: The government forwards the project to the National Assembly at the beginning of the session, with its explanatory memorandum and annexes.
Commission: hearings then review article by article, for three to four weeks.
Public session: debate, amendments and vote, for one to two weeks.
Senate: examination in turn, with a mixed commission in the event of disagreement between the two chambers.
Final adoption: promulgation and publication, for application on January 1.

body.text: Technical work takes place in committee. Members of Parliament who are members interview the administrations and question program managers on the use of credits. The education, health or public works services explain what they spent and what they are asking for. Members then table amendments. An amendment modifies an article of the text. It is only admissible if it respects the balance of the budget. In public session, all the deputies resume the discussion. The debates are in principle public and give rise to a report.
In committee, we read the budget line by line. What seems abstract in a speech becomes concrete: how many classrooms, how many dispensaries, how many kilometers of road.
body.attribution: Ludovic Mpaga, MP, Member of the Finance Committee

body.text: The Senate then receives the voted text. He examines it in turn, first in committee, then in session. He can modify it. If the two chambers do not agree, a joint commission, made up of members of each, seeks a joint drafting. The calendar is intended for adoption before the end of the calendar year, as the budget applies from January 1 to December 31. If time is running out, transitional measures allow the State to continue to pay its agents and suppliers.
What the budget contains

A budget of this size can be read in large masses. On the revenue side, it is based on oil revenues, taxes and duties, customs duties and, to complete the balance, on loans. On the expenditure side, in the example chosen, the salaries of public officials represent approximately 1,000 billion FCFA. Goods, services and transfers weigh 900, and as many investments. The debt service, interest and repayments included, reached 1,200 billion. These amounts are orders of magnitude. In a real project, each line is detailed by program, with objectives and outcome indicators.

body.label: Order of magnitude of the expenses of a finance bill

body.text: Three priorities are displayed in the example: school, health and roads. They cross several blocks at the same time: teacher and caregiver salaries, purchases of textbooks and drugs, maintenance of the road network. As an indication, education would represent around 15% of expenses, health 8% and roads 6%. MEPs compare these shares from one year to the next and ask what explains the gaps. An announced but little-funded project is quickly spotted when reading the lines.
Parliament authorizes the budget, *He doesn't write it*. It can reduce credits, redirect them, require explanations. But the rules of admissibility limit its ability to create new expenses.
body.attribution: Aurélie Ndembi, research professor in public law

body.text: What citizens can follow

The budget is not reserved for specialists. Public sessions can be followed, and reports consulted after the fact. The project is accompanied by explanatory documents: hypotheses retained, distribution of appropriations, objectives by public policy. During the year, an amending finance law can adjust the amounts. The following year, a settlement law compares what was voted and what was actually spent.

There remains the question of execution: a voted credit is not a credit spent. Following the gap between the two, project by project, is a concrete way to read a budget. Our analyzes are brought together in the section [public finances](/rubrique/economie/finances-publiques).

english.title: Decentralisation: what new powers mean for municipalities
english.dek: From civil registration and roads to markets and waste collection, decentralisation gives municipalities new responsibilities. Here is what changes for funding, staff and timetables, from the council chamber to the service counter.
keyPoints: The transfer entrusts four daily services to the municipalities: civil status, roads, markets and waste collection.
A skill does not transfer alone: it supposes an endowment of the State, trained agents and material.
At the counter, the inhabitants keep a local interlocutor, but deadlines and prices may vary from one municipality to another.

seo.description: Civil status, roads, markets, waste: what the transfer of powers from the State to the municipalities changes for the inhabitants and the local finances.

body.text: Transferring a skill is changing the name of the one who answers the inhabitant. In the context of decentralization, services now provided or supervised by the State come under the responsibility of the municipalities: civil status, roads, markets, waste collection. The municipality becomes the direct interlocutor, the State accompanies it and finances part of it. To fix the ideas, let's imagine a municipality the size of a provincial capital, like Lambaréné, on the banks of the Ogooué. What changes for her is, with nuances, for the other municipalities of the country.
Four daily services

The civil status covers the registration of births, marriages and deaths, and the issuance of copies of acts. It's a visible service: enrollment in school or access to care depends on it. The roads are the streets, the gutters and the lighting of the districts; The main axes remain in principle the jurisdiction of the State. The markets involve stalls, water, sanitary facilities and the collection of place rights. Finally, waste collection goes through bins, trucks and a deposit place. These are services that the inhabitant uses every week, often without knowing who is responsible for it.

At the counter, the inhabitant does not ask who is competent. He wants his birth certificate, a passable street, a clean market. Once the competence is transferred, it is up to the municipality to answer, and it is towards it that we will turn if it does not work.
body.attribution: Ghislaine Ndjoungui, municipal councilor in a medium-sized municipality

body.text: means transferred with the skills

The principle is simple: no competence without means. The State pays an endowment, which the municipality completes with its own revenue: place duties, local taxes, royalties. It also makes agents available to the municipality and organizes their training. These agents generally keep their status, seniority and remuneration. The municipality then has a wider budget, but also new charges: salaries, fuel, equipment maintenance, contracts with service providers. The challenge is to adjust to each other, service by service.

body.label: indicative part of the State's expenditure paid to the municipalities in the form of allocations

body.text: Not all municipalities start from the same level. A provincial capital collects more place rights than a small rural town. To prevent the gap to widen, part of the endowment takes into account the population, the extent of the territory and the length of the routes to be maintained, and not only the local revenue. This mechanism, called equalization, reduces deviations without removing them. Municipalities with limited resources thus receive a higher share per inhabitant.

*A transfer without resources* Only available on paper. The right question is not who is competent, but with what budget, what agents and what equipment. A municipality that inherits a competence without the corresponding means retains a responsibility that it cannot exercise.
body.attribution: Brice Tsamba, local finance consultant

body.text: What changes at the counter

The transfer does not take place in a day. A typical calendar is spread over three years: marital status and markets the first year, roads the second, waste collection the third. Each stage begins with an inventory of existing means, then with an agreement between the State and the municipality. Agents are trained before the relay is taken. During the transfer period, the old services continue to respond to users. At the end of each year, a report compares the means transferred and the service rendered. For the inhabitant, the expected changes are concrete:

items: Requests for civil status documents are filed and withdrawn at the town hall, according to deadlines displayed at the counter.
Place rights and collection fees may be set by the municipal council, within the limits provided for by the texts.
Claims are brought before the municipality, whose council meets in public session.
The municipal budget can be consulted by the inhabitants, as well as the decisions of the council.

body.text: For the inhabitants, the test will be simple: an act issued within a known time, a maintained street, a clean market. The municipalities will have to be accountable to their municipal council and to the citizens who follow its meetings. The State retains a role of control and support, in particular for the training of agents. Everyone can also question their municipal councilors on the use of endowments. Our section [territories](/rubrique/politique/territoires) follows these reforms at the local level.

english.title: Maritime security: Gulf of Guinea countries meet in Libreville
english.dek: Experts from countries bordering the Gulf of Guinea spent three days in Libreville discussing illegal fishing, information sharing and joint patrols. The technical meeting prepares recommendations for policymakers.
keyPoints: About fifty experts from countries bordering the Gulf of Guinea met three days in Libreville for a technical workshop.
Illicit fishing, information sharing and joint patrols were included in the program, as part of the 2013 Yaoundé Summit architecture.
The workshop does not make any decision: it produces recommendations, which each country will examine on its side.

seo.description: Illicit fishing, information sharing, joint patrols: experts from the Gulf of Guinea gathered in Libreville on maritime security.

body.text: About fifty experts, from around ten countries bordering the Gulf of Guinea, met three days in Libreville for a workshop devoted to maritime security. Navy officers, coast guards, fisheries administrators and lawyers worked on three subjects: illicit fishing, information sharing and joint patrols. This is a technical meeting. It produces neither treaty nor decision, but recommendations that each country will then examine for its part. Delegations compared their practices and listed concrete obstacles to joint action.
A regional framework already in place

The regional cooperation is based on the architecture from the Yaoundé Summit in 2013. This divides the surveillance into maritime zones, plans regional coordination centers and organizes the exchange of information between States. It targets piracy, but also other illicit activities at sea: trafficking, pollution, undeclared fishing. The workshop did not question this framework. He sought to make it more concrete, with work procedures that the teams could apply on a daily basis: who warns who, in what time frame, with what means.
illicit fishing, a shortfall

Illicit, unreported and unregulated fishing, deprives receipts and impoverishes fish stocks, on which many coastal families also depend. It is often practiced far from the coast, where a ship can cut its positioning beacon and resume its route without being seen. Each state first monitors its exclusive economic zone, which extends up to 200 nautical miles from the shore. No country in the region can cover it on its own at all times. Pooling satellite images and ship positions makes it possible to identify unusual behavior more quickly.

body.label: indicative part of the catches of the region which escape any declaration

body.text: A ship that cuts its beacon on the high seas is only visible if a neighbor shares his radar or satellite images. An isolated position does not say much. pooling with others, it becomes *an alert*.
body.attribution: Arsène Moukala, frigate captain, naval officer

body.text: Information sharing and joint patrols

Information sharing involves a common language: data formats, transmission delays, privacy levels. An alert sent too late is useless. A message that is too widely distributed can, on the contrary, prevent the one we were trying to identify. The experts therefore worked on simple sheets, which can be used at night by a coordination center operator, with the same sections from one country to another. They also mentioned the training: an operator who knows how to read a map of positions more quickly identify what is out of the ordinary.

The joint patrols occupied a whole day. Can a ship from a country operate in the waters of a neighbor? Experts have studied the formula of an on-board liaison officer, who represents the waterfront on board and authorizes an intervention. They also talked about image exchange, common working languages, patrol calendars and fuel costs sharing. Each point presupposes a written agreement between states, therefore legal work.

Artisan fishermen know the sea, but not always the rules that change. We do not ask to be protected from everything. We ask that we explain where the reserved areas are and that we are listened to before fixing them.
body.attribution: Noëlle Mayombo, head of the Mer and Lagoon cooperative

body.text: Several fishermen's cooperatives had been invited. Their presence responds to a reality: artisanal fishermen are often the first witnesses to what is happening near the coasts. Participants proposed a simple signaling device, by radio or by telephone, to a coordination center, with feedback to the fishermen. The cooperatives also ask that the reserved areas be marked and the rules are explained in simple terms.

The recommendations of the workshop will be sent to the competent authorities of each country. A new technical meeting is planned in six months, to measure what can be applied without delay. No decision date is set: each state remains free from its calendar. The other meetings of regional cooperation are followed in the section [Diplomacy](/rubrique/politique/diplomatie).

english.title: Civil registration: pilot programme digitises birth certificates
english.dek: Paper registers are deteriorating, copies take time to obtain and some children have no birth certificate. A pilot programme is digitising civil registration records. We look at its timetable, data protection and what families expect.
keyPoints: The pilot phase scans the birth records of a few civil status centers and records new births online.
The objective is to reduce the number of children without birth certificates and to shorten the time to issue copies.
The protection of the personal data of children and families conditions the extension of the device.

seo.description: The digitization of birth certificates enters the pilot phase: objectives, centers concerned, calendar and protection of personal data.

body.text: In about ten civil status centers, birth registers begin to be digitized. This pilot phase, scheduled for six months, tests three operations: the entry of old registers, the registration of new births at the maternity ward and the issuance of copies of acts from any participating center. The centers are equipped with computers and scanners, and their agents have been trained for a few days. A senatorial commission interviewed technicians on the reform, in order to understand the device: timing, costs, data security.
Why scan

A birth certificate opens access to school, care and administrative procedures. However, some children do not have one, for lack of a declaration on time, by distance from the civil status center or because of the cost of the steps. For a child whose birth has not been declared in time, the regularization generally goes through a legal procedure, often long. The paper registers pose another problem: humidity, erasures, misplaced volumes. Finding an act can take several days. The digital copy should make it possible to find it in a few minutes, while the paper register remains the official reference.

body.label: order of magnitude on the part of children under five without birth certificates

body.text: When a register is damaged, it is a piece of the history of a district that fades. With a digital copy, I find an act in a few minutes instead of several days. But I continue to check each information with the family, at the counter.
body.attribution: Pascaline Itoungou, civil status officer

body.text: For a family, the difference is measured in travel. Today, getting a copy may require going to the center where the birth was recorded, sometimes several hours away. With the pilot device, the copy is requested at any participating center. Rural families thus avoid a long journey and a lost day of work. The applicant must, however, appear with an identity document, and the signature of the civil registrar remains necessary.
What the pilot phase is testing
The device is based on three components, evaluated separately, each with its own indicators:

items: Resumption of paper registers: each act is entered, then checked by a second agent, before being attached to the original register.
Maternity birth registration: an opinion is transmitted electronically to the civil status centre.
Copies of deeds: They are issued from any pilot center, with a verification code printed on the document.

body.text: The centers chosen are urban and rural, spread over several provinces. This choice makes it possible to test the operation with a sometimes unstable connection and limited equipment. After six months, an assessment will measure delivery times, number of acts seized, error rate, system availability and user satisfaction. Families will be asked about the length of the process and the clarity of the explanations received. A gradual extension could follow over two years, center by center, if the results are conclusive and if the means follow.
Protect family data

Digitizing is also concentrating. A birth certificate file contains names, dates, filiations. The rules provided for the pilot phase are based on simple principles: access reserved for authorized agents, tracing of each consultation, secure accommodation, fixed retention period, right of rectification for families. Each agent has a personal identifier, and backups are kept outside the center. The data is only used for civil status: any other use requires a specific legal framework. The technicians heard in the Senate detailed these measures and their cost.

A birth certificate keeps a lifetime. Scanning is useful if it remains *A tool for families*. It must be said who has access to the data, for how long, and how to correct an error. And it has to be told to families in simple terms.
body.attribution: Clément Pambou, jurist at the association A name for each

body.text: The pilot phase does not cut everything. The centers will have to verify that remote families access the service, including without a connection, and that agents do not end up with two registers to keep instead of one. The lessons will be used to decide on a possible generalization. The other ongoing reforms are followed in the section [Government](/rubrique/politique/gouvernement).

rentree-scolaire-salles-de-classe-effect.dek: Dans une école publique de Libreville, les huit salles de classe ont été remises en état pendant les vacances. Les classes restent pourtant pleines, deux postes d'enseignants sont vacants et les fournitures pèsent sur les familles.

english.authorBio: She investigates school, health and daily life, and recounts the Gabonese cultural scene, from museums to the studios of Libreville.
english.title: Back to school: renovated classrooms are still crowded
english.dek: Eight classrooms at a public school in Libreville were refurbished during the holidays. Classes are still full, two teaching posts remain vacant and school supplies strain family budgets.
keyPoints: At the Frangipani public school, in Libreville, the eight classrooms were restored during the holidays: roofs, floors, lighting and paintings.
With about 640 students for twelve classes, the average number exceeds fifty students, and four rooms serve twice a day thanks to the double vacation.
Two teaching positions remain vacant, and supplies cost families from 30,000 to 50,000 FCFA per child.

seo.description: Report in a public school in Libreville: renovated rooms, double vacation, vacancy and cost of supplies for families at the start of the school year.

body.text: Seven o'clock, in the courtyard of the Frangipaniers' public school, in Libreville. The smell of fresh paint still floats in front of the main building. The morning students line up in classes, satchel on their backs, under the eyes of the masters. A bell, a whistle, and the ranks enter the rooms. Those of the afternoon, they will only arrive at noon. Here, the start of the school year has two faces: walls refurbished, and numbers that have hardly moved.
Rehabilitated rooms

During the summer holidays, the eight classrooms were rehabilitated. The sheet metal roofs have been replaced, the ceilings taken over, the tiled floors. The electrical installation has been brought up to standard, the tables and table-benchs changed. In the yard, the water point is working again and the two toilet blocks have been resumed. The construction site, of the order of 45 million FCFA, was completed a few days before the resumption of classes. Under the courtyard, a colored frieze, painted by the teachers, replaces the traces of humidity. On rainy days, the water no longer flows on the benches.
A child learns better when the roof is not leaking and the painting reads from the back of the class. It is an achievement. But a redone room with fifty students in it remains *An overloaded room*.
body.attribution: Honorine Mapangou, director of the Frangipaniers public school

body.text: Full classes, missing masters

The school has about 640 students, divided into twelve classes. However, it only has eight rooms. Four of them therefore serve twice a day: a CP or CE class works there in the morning, from 7:30 a.m. to noon, then a CM class succeeds it, from noon and a half to 5 p.m. It's the double shift. It imposes staggered hours on families, especially when two brothers or sisters are out of school at the same time.

body.label: Average enrollment per class in the school: approximately 640 students for twelve classes

body.text: The lack of teachers weighs on this daily life. Two positions have remained vacant since the start of the school year, a CE1 and a CM2. During the first few weeks, the colleagues took turns to take the courses. temporary workers now help out, but their presence is not always regular. When one of them is missing, the students are distributed in the neighboring classes, and some settle in three on a table planned for two. The management hopes for the assignment of two holders before the end of the quarter.
At fifty students, we do not follow each child. I correct fewer notebooks, I give less individual exercises. We manage a group, we no longer teach everyone.
body.attribution: Évariste Ibinga, teacher in CM1

body.text: What does the return to school cost for families?

At home, the start of the school year can be counted in tickets. Notebooks, books, slate, blouse, bag, shoes: the list given to parents is long. For a child, the bill is between 30,000 and 50,000 FCFA depending on purchases. The total climbs quickly in families where several children are educated. Many spread out the expenses or retrieve the textbooks of the elders. Some first buy the notebooks and push the rest back to the end of the month.

The school seeks to limit the expense. The list was brought back to basics, and the teachers agreed on identical notebooks from one class to another. The parents' association organizes a barter of used books in the courtyard, every Saturday of the start of the school year. Families also come to exchange blouses and bags.

With three children at school, the start of the school year is about a month's salary. We buy in several times, we borrow, we take second-hand. The new walls are good. But they are masters in front of the classes that families expect.
body.attribution: Joël Ntoutoume, father of three school children

body.text: At noon, the bell rings. The afternoon students enter the yard as the morning students come out. The rolling starts again. The director would like these redone walls to house, one day, less busy classes. The follow-up of the start of the school year and its means continues in our section [Education](/rubrique/societe/education).

english.title: Malaria: mosquito net distribution begins in Moyen-Ogooué
english.dek: A campaign is taking insecticide-treated mosquito nets door to door in Lambaréné and by canoe to villages along the river. Its success will depend on whether people use the nets every night.
keyPoints: A campaign to distribute mosquito nets impregnated with insecticide starts in the Middle Ogooué: door to door in Lambaréné, by canoe in the villages of the river.
About 38,000 mosquito nets are planned, at the rate of one for two people, for a province of approximately 75,000 inhabitants.
Community health workers install mosquito nets with families, then come back to check that they are used properly.

seo.description: In the Middle Ogooué, a campaign distributes impregnated mosquito nets, from door-to-door to canoes. The challenge: that they serve every night.

body.text: Six hours, on the bank of the Ogooué, in Lambaréné. In the mist, two motorized canoes load blue plastic bundles. Four community health workers, yellow vest on their backs, wedge the packages under tarpaulins. On the platform, the checklist passes from hand to hand: a bundle, two bales, three. Each bundle contains dozens of insecticide-treated mosquito nets. Direction the villages upstream: two hours of ascent, more if the level of the river is low.

The campaign started this week in the Middle Ogooué. The objective: a mosquito net for two people in each household, or approximately 38,000 rooms for a province of around 75,000. The river health collective, which brings together local associations, coordinates the operation. Its warehouse is located in Lambaréné, a few minutes walk from the Albert-Schweitzer Hospital. About sixty community health workers spread the territory for three weeks, with around forty villages to reach by the river or by the track. Each handed net is written on the household sheet, with the number of beds and people to be protected.
From door-to-door to canoes

Logistics is patience. The mosquito nets arrive by truck from Libreville, then are divided by zone. In Lambaréné, the agents knock on the doors, district after quarter, with a list of households and a pointing notebook. They visit about thirty homes a day in town, only about ten on the river, where distances are lengthening. Each agent takes few things: a vest, a notebook, a rope, a few nails, and an unfolded mosquito net for the demonstration. Depending on the season, a village meets in two hours or four. It is sometimes necessary to unload the bundles on the bank, carry them, then reload them further.

The mosquito nets are not heavy, it is the volume that clutters. When the canoe is full, we no longer see the front. So we leave early, we stop where we need, and we count the bundles at each stopover.
body.attribution: Prosper Mavoungou, pirogue

body.label: planned quantity for the province, at the rate of one mosquito net for two people

body.text: Distributing is not enough

A mosquito net only protects if it is suspended above the bed, every night, and if its edges fit under the mattress. On the ground, the teams encounter several obstacles, all concrete. Three often come up during check visits:

items: The mosquito net remains in its packaging, kept for later or for a big occasion
The heat encourages you to sleep without it, or outside, when the air is heavy and the power is off
The bed is too wide, or the ceiling too low, to hang it properly

body.text: We do not deposit the mosquito net to leave. We hang it with the family, we check that the edges fit under the mattress, we explain who should sleep under: children under five and pregnant women first. Then we come back in the month, we look, we ask.
body.attribution: Arlette Nzigou, community health worker

body.label: Share of households visited during a previous passage where the received mosquito net was suspended above a bed

body.text: A second passage to check

The second passage is part of the device. About a month after the first passage, the teams will redo the journey in the opposite direction, village after village. They will count the suspended mosquito nets, not those that have been distributed. They will also note the condition of each mosquito net, will replace those which are torn within the limit of the remaining stock, and will recall a few gestures: wash it rarely, without rubbing it, dry it in the shade. They will finally recall a reflex: in case of fever, especially in a child, you have to consult without delay. A quick test allows you to know if malaria is involved.

The agents know it: the result will not be measured by the number of bundles unloaded, but, in a few months, by the number of cases of fever in the villages. Other field reports on prevention are gathered in our section [Health](/rubrique/societe/sante).

emploi-jeunes-apprentissage-entreprise-p.title: Emploi des jeunes : l'apprentissage en entreprise à l'épreuve du terrain
emploi-jeunes-apprentissage-entreprise-p.dek: Un an après son lancement, le programme d'apprentissage « Pierre à Pierre » débouche sur une embauche pour près de six jeunes sur dix de la première promotion. Tutorat, indemnités et transport restent à régler.

english.authorBio: It covers infrastructure, logistics, employment and public procurement. He worked for six years in transport consulting before joining the press.
english.title: Youth employment: putting apprenticeships to the test
english.dek: A year after its launch, the Pierre à Pierre apprenticeship programme has led to jobs for nearly six in ten members of its first intake. Mentoring, allowances and transport still need funding.
keyPoints: A year after its launch, the "Pierre à Pierre" apprenticeship program has around 420 young people in around thirty construction companies.
Nearly six out of ten apprentices from the first promotion were hired by the company that had trained them.
The guardians lack time, the allowances are reimbursed late to the companies and the transport weighs on the budget of the apprentices.

seo.description: Apprenticeship "Pierre à Pierre": nearly six out of ten young people hired at the exit, but tutoring, allowances and transport get stuck. first assessment.

body.text: On the construction site of a three-storey building, in Libreville, we first hear the concrete mixer. Cement dust sticks to boots. Then the voice of a team leader, who has a wall taken again: he is not in balance. In front of him, a young woman corrects her alignment with the plumb line and starts again. Lydie Nkoghe is 22 years old. She has been an apprentice mason for nine months at Komo Bâtiment, a small company of fourteen employees.

She is one of some 420 young people who entered "Pierre à Pierre", a learning program launched a year ago by a group of companies and training centers. The principle is simple: three days a week on a construction site, two days in the room, for twelve months. The courses focus on reading plans, calculating quantities and safety. Apprentices are between 18 and 25 years old. About thirty companies, especially SMEs, welcome them. The program follow-up committee has just published an initial assessment.
Hirings at the exit

It is the result that holds the attention. The program opened three successive entries of 140 young people each, but only the first completed its twelve-month cycle: the other two are still in training, which invites caution. For this first promotion, nearly six out of ten young people were hired by the company that had formed them. others have joined a neighboring company or a subcontractor.

body.label: Share of apprentices from the first promotion hired at the end of the cycle by their host company
body.source: Follow-up committee of the "Pierre à Pierre" program

body.text: For employers, the interest is in one sentence: they recruit young people whose work they already know. They also save time, because an apprentice trained in the methods of the house is operational as soon as he is hired. At Komo Bâtiment, three of the five apprentices welcomed signed a contract at the end of the cycle. The other two chose to continue their training.

An apprentice I trained for a year, I know what it's worth, and he knows how we work. I would not have taken this risk by recruiting at random. And for the young, it is *A real job* At the exit, not another course.
body.attribution: Gaspard Nziengui, manager of Komo Building

body.text: Tutors, allowances, transport: what gets stuck

The difficulties focus on three points. First tutoring: each apprentice is followed by an experienced employee, without this training time being deducted from his production. Then the compensation, of around 60,000 FCFA per month. The company advances it, and the reimbursement occurs only after several weeks, which weighs on the cash flow of small structures. Finally, transport, which remains the responsibility of young people.

I'm a tutor, but that's in addition to my work. When you pour a slab or a delivery arrives, I don't have time to explain. The apprentice is waiting, or he does it alone. This tutoring time should be expected, and recognized.
body.attribution: Hilaire Mouity, site manager and tutor

body.label: Estimated cost of transporting an apprentice who lives on the outskirts, for compensation of around 60,000 FCFA

body.text: For apprentices who live on the outskirts, the journey is a charge. Lydie Nkoghe takes two taxis on the way out and two on the way back. She leaves her home at 5:45 a.m. to be on site at 7 a.m. Some mornings, she counts her pieces before leaving. She arrives tired, but says hold: she likes the job. Faced with these difficulties, the monitoring committee indicates that it is working on three avenues for the next promotion:

items: A tutoring bonus, to compensate for the time spent with apprentices
a reimbursement of compensation by mobile transfer, within a period set in advance
Group transport from outlying districts to construction sites

body.text: Nothing is acquired. Companies are waiting for specific deadlines, young people an affordable journey. On one point, however, the experiment has proven itself: a young person trained on the construction site finds his place in the company more easily. The monitoring committee announces a fourth entry, open to trades other than masonry: plumbing, electricity, carpentry. The training and integration offers are brought together in our section [Employment](/rubrique/societe/emploi).

english.title: Neighbourhood football: a Libreville school trains on the beach
english.dek: Without a pitch, the Étoile du Rivage association coaches around forty young people on the sand. Volunteers run the sessions, pupils bring school reports each term, and every ball is accounted for.
keyPoints: For lack of available land, the Étoile du Rivage association is training around forty young people on a beach in Libreville.
To play, each child must be educated and present their newsletter each term: the school comes before the ball.
Led by volunteers, the association lacks balls, chasubles and goals, and is looking for partners to equip themselves.

seo.description: In Libreville, the Étoile du Rivage association trains around forty young footballers on the beach, with volunteers and a rule: school first.

body.text: Sixteen-thirty, the tide descends. On a beach on the coast of Libreville, the sand becomes firm and the ground appears. Two wooden stakes and a rope serve as a goal. Flip flops mark the sidelines. About forty young people arrive running, ball under their arm. In a few minutes, the shore star association training begins, barefoot for many.

The association was founded six years ago by former players from the neighborhood. The first training sessions brought together a dozen children; Word of mouth did the rest. It now welcomes 42 young people aged 8 to 16, girls and boys, divided into three age groups. The clay court where once played has disappeared under constructions. Only the beach remained, accessible on foot from the nearby alleys.
A land that the sea takes up twice a day

The tide dictates the program. The sessions take place three times a week, at the end of the afternoon after class, and on Saturday mornings, with a schedule that slips a few tens of minutes depending on the tide. At high tide, there is only a narrow strip of sand: the short passes and the head game are worked on it. At low tide, we play seven against seven. At the other end of the beach, a net of volleyball serves as a landmark. We share the space with the volleyball players, in turn. The goal pickets sleep with a neighbor, who keeps them in his yard.

On the sand, a young man learns to control the ball, to keep his balance, to raise his head. We run slower, but we work on the technique. Only, you need equipment: balls, goals, chasubles. Today, we do with what we have.
body.attribution: Rodrigue Mintsa, volunteer educator of the association

body.text: A session lasts an hour and a half. Warm-up, ball driving between sand-filled bottles, triangle passing games, then a match. 8-10 year olds are relaying, older groups are working on their placement in the field. Educators correct little and encourage a lot. At the end, everyone picks up the waste left on the beach, before walking home.
The school first

In star of the shore, a rule takes precedence over all the others: to train, you have to be educated. Parents submit the newsletter at the start of each term. A child without a ballot remains on the bench until regularization. When the grades drop, the volunteers offer tutoring one evening a week, led by a retired teacher. The contribution is 2,000 FCFA per month; Families who cannot pay for it are exempt.
My son knows his lessons before going to training. He knows that without a bulletin, there is no session. At home, we no longer argue about homework. Football has become *a reason to do them*.
body.attribution: Estelle Ndombi, mother of a player

body.text: Nine volunteers, little equipment

The association is based on nine volunteers: educators, a retired teacher, parents who provide support and snacks. Everyone gives a few hours a week. The material is counted: a dozen worn balloons, mismatched chasubles, a single game of small goals damaged by salt. At the beginning of each session, a volunteer notes the number of balloons. At the end, he counts.

body.label: Amount needed to equip the school: balloons, chasubles, two small goals and a first aid kit

body.text: The association is looking for partners, businesses in the neighborhood or individuals, to equip themselves. A trader offered six balloons at the start of the school year, but the wear is quick: the sand wears the seams and the salt damages the coating. Ultimately, the volunteers would like a hard field, even small, to continue to play on high tide days. In the meantime, the sand does the trick, and it requires a more technical game.

At the final whistle, the group line up. The balloons are counted, one by one. None should stay on the sand: the rising tide would prevail. Local football initiatives are brought together in our section [Football](/rubrique/sport/football).

english.title: Running: 3,000 expected for Libreville’s seafront 10K
english.dek: The Foulées de l’Estuaire association is organising a 10-kilometre race along the Libreville seafront. Here is what to know about the flat route, the 5,000 CFA franc entry fee and the amateur clubs taking part.
keyPoints: The Foulées de l'Estuaire association is organizing a 10-kilometer race for the first time on the Libreville seafront, with around 3,000 participants expected.
The course is flat, the start is given at 6:30 a.m. to avoid the heat, and the bib costs 5,000 FCFA, with a 5-kilometer walk in parallel.
The amateur clubs have been preparing beginners for several weeks, with simple advice: progress in stages, drink, leave slowly.

seo.description: 10 km from the seafront in Libreville: routes, registrations at 5,000 FCFA, amateur clubs and advice for running safely before departure.

body.text: It is 5:45 a.m. and the seafront is still only a gray band. However, around sixty runners are already warming up on the sidewalk, headlamp on. The beams sweep the asphalt. This Sunday, the amateur clubs spot the course of the 10 km of the seafront, the start of which will be given in a few weeks. On the one hand, the Atlantic Ocean. on the other, the awakening city. In front, a straight line that no one looks at without calculating its pace.

For its first edition, the Foulées de l'Estuaire association expects 3,000 runners. She chose the formula for a popular race: timed for those who wish, open to beginners, walkers and clubs. Several coastal amateur clubs have already registered their members. The start is set at 6:30 a.m., before the heat, in front of a village on the seafront. The arrival is judged at the same place, with supplies, first aid station and entertainment.
courses and registrations

The route is flat: a 5-kilometre round trip along the sea, to be covered twice. Three water points line the course, approximately every 2.5 kilometers, and a refueling waits at the finish. Traffic will be diverted on the route during the morning, say the organizers. Rapid runners will complete the 10 km in less than forty minutes, the others in an hour or more. The time limit is set at 1h30, i.e. an average pace of about 6.7 km/h.

body.label: participants expected for this first edition, including a large part of beginners

body.text: Registrations are done online or at three points of sale distributed in the city. The bib costs 5,000 FCFA, and 3,000 FCFA for students and job seekers, on proof. He retired the day before, between 3 p.m. and 7 p.m., in the village of the race. A 5 kilometer walk, without a stopwatch, leaves at 7 a.m. for those who prefer not to run.

We wanted a race where the one who completes the 10 km in fifty minutes and the one who takes twenty minutes, alternating walking and running, find themselves on the same starting line. The objective is not the clock. It's from *make you want to move*.
body.attribution: Mireille Moussounda, volunteer organizer of Foulées de l'Estuaire

body.text: Amateur clubs, engines of preparation

For several weeks, coastal clubs have been preparing their members. Tide pace and Komo mornings organize group outings three mornings a week, before work. They offer beginners an eight-week plan: alternating walking and running, then gradual lengthening of running times. The groups are mixed, the levels mixed, so that no one runs alone. Those who prefer to walk also have their group, which is aiming for the 5 kilometer walk.

I started a year ago with ten minutes of running interspersed with walking. Today I last an hour. In the morning, before work, I feel that my breath and my sleep have changed. The first week was difficult, but the group carried me.
body.attribution: Prisca Engonga, amateur runner

body.text: Running without danger

Running to the seaside also means dealing with heat and humidity, from dawn. Regular activity, even moderate, benefits the heart and sleep, remind the coaches, provided they progress in stages. They summarize a few simple rules:

items: Ask a doctor's advice in case of doubt: high blood pressure, heart history, resumption after a long break
Drink regularly the day before and on the morning of the race, without excess
Running with shoes already worn, never new on D-Day
Leaving slowly: the first two kilometers should look easy
Stop and notify a volunteer in case of discomfort or pain in the chest

body.text: For the organizers, success will be measured less by the number of bibs than with what will follow: groups that continue to run, inhabitants who take a liking to movement, and perhaps a second edition. Other amateur meetings are gathered in our section [Other disciplines](/rubrique/sport/autres-disciplines).

ecotourisme-parcs-nationaux-pari-gabonai.dek: Treize parcs, une forêt qui couvre environ 88 % du pays, des éléphants que l'on croise jusque sur la plage de Loango : l'atout est rare. Reste à le rendre accessible, abordable et utile aux villages riverains.

english.authorBio: He covers national parks and the coast for the Tourism section, and follows Gabonese sport from neighbourhood football to national competitions.
english.title: Ecotourism: Gabon’s national park gamble
english.dek: Thirteen national parks, forests covering about 88% of the country, and elephants that venture onto Loango’s beach give Gabon a rare advantage. The challenge is to make the parks accessible and affordable while ensuring that nearby villages benefit.
keyPoints: Gabon has thirteen national parks. Established in 2002, they cover nearly 11% of the country and offer opportunities to see wildlife, especially in Loango.
Difficult access, costly domestic travel, limited accommodation and uneven guide training hold back visitor numbers.
Tour operators want clearer rules and regular transport links. Villages bordering the parks want steadier economic benefits.

seo.description: Thirteen national parks and abundant wildlife, alongside costly travel and limited accommodation. A closer look at Gabon’s ecotourism ambitions.

body.text: At Loango, elephants use the beach as a path. Late in the day, an adult emerges from the forest, crosses the sand slowly, pauses at the surf and heads back towards the trees. Farther along, two buffalo watch. In the lagoon, a hippopotamus leaves only its eyes and nostrils above water. On the terrace of a nearby lodge, visitors hold their breath. No one wants to make a sound. The scene is entirely natural. It captures the gamble Gabon took when it established its national parks in 2002: to turn its forests and wildlife into a lasting source of income without harming them. The natural setting is already there. The economy that can sustain it still needs to be built.

body.caption: Forest elephants at the edge of the savannah in Loango National Park.

body.text: The numbers show the scale of Gabon’s natural assets. Its thirteen national parks, established in 2002, cover nearly 11% of the country. Forest covers about 88%. Two protected areas are UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Lopé-Okanda since 2007 and Ivindo since 2021. Along the coast at Loango, elephants, buffalo and hippos can be seen even on the beach. Across from Libreville, where the forest meets the ocean in Pongara National Park, leatherback turtles come ashore to nest from roughly November to March. These natural assets give people a clear reason to visit, but building a tourism industry takes more. Wildlife roams freely and sightings cannot be scheduled. Operators are selling visitors the time and opportunity to encounter wildlife, with no guaranteed show. The professionals interviewed for this story pointed to the same obstacles.

body.caption: The savannahs and forests of Lopé, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007.

body.label: National parks established in 2002, covering nearly 11% of the country

body.text: The barriers: access, cost, accommodation and guides

Distance is the first obstacle. Reaching the most remote parks from Libreville may mean combining a flight, a road journey and a canoe trip, sometimes taking an entire day. There are exceptions. The Pointe-Denis peninsula is about twenty minutes from Libreville by boat and easy to visit over a weekend, although it offers only a glimpse of what the parks have to offer. For other sites, distance drives up the price. Operators say domestic transport often costs as much as the stay itself, and five days in a park can cost more than one million CFA francs per person. Accommodation is the second obstacle. Lodges and camps near the parks are estimated to offer about 400 beds across roughly thirty establishments. One group can fill an entire site. The properties are small and often isolated, and some close outside the season because they lack a steady flow of guests. Their small size limits pressure on the sites, but also caps revenue.

body.label: Estimated total capacity of lodges and camps near the parks
body.source: Approximate figure for this demonstration article

body.text: *A visitor pays twice*: first for the stay, then for the journey. The journey sometimes costs more. We cannot cut our prices without lowering quality, and we have no control over transport costs.
body.attribution: Hortense MBOUMBA, manager of the Passe-aux-Hérons lodge

body.text: A less visible obstacle is guide training. Ecoguides are the public face of the parks. They read tracks, anticipate encounters and protect visitors and animals alike. Much of their training takes place in the field, with short courses that vary in quality from site to site. ‘They teach us how to identify species,’ says Landry MABIKA, an ecoguide for nine years. ‘We get less practice in explaining the forest, managing a tired group or speaking English after three days of rain.’ Several operators want an accredited programme with different levels so young people can build a career across seasons. They say too many trained guides leave after a few years because they see no prospect of a stable income.
What operators need and what villages stand to gain

Operators agree on what they need: regular air, river or road links to visitor destinations, and enough advance notice of visiting rules and access dates to sell trips a year ahead. They want guides trained to a common standard and coordinated investment in tracks and landing stages. Several also suggest pooling overseas promotion, which each property currently handles on its own. ‘We’re looking for a kind of tourism where we can promise a date and a price and stick to both,’ says Sidonie AYINGONE, who runs an inbound travel agency in Libreville. ‘We aren’t looking for mass tourism.’ For operators, reliability matters as much as price. People booking a trip from abroad may give up at the first sign of uncertainty.
We used to get only fish from the lagoon. Now taking visitors out in a canoe pays for a day’s work. When there are no visitors, there’s nothing. We need it to last all year.
body.attribution: Félicien MAPANGOU, canoe operator in a village bordering a national park

body.text: Villages bordering the parks do benefit, though the gains are modest and seasonal. Canoe operators, cooks, craft workers and a handful of guides earn extra income. People we interviewed said that some lodges buy smoked fish and vegetables locally and pay a levy into a village fund. In one village near a park, a committee of craft workers and canoe operators now shares visits among families to spread the work. Living alongside wildlife takes work. The elephants that draw visitors sometimes trample cassava and banana crops. If Gabon’s gamble is to pay off, the parks will have to benefit the people who live on their doorstep as much as they appeal to visitors. We’ll continue this reporting in our [National parks](/rubrique/tourisme/parcs-nationaux) section.

english.title: Pointe-Denis: a weekend of beaches and leatherback turtles near Libreville
english.dek: A boat ride, pale sand and a night-time outing to watch leatherback turtles nest. This guide covers a weekend on the peninsula, including visitor rules and estimated costs.
keyPoints: The Pointe-Denis is joined by boat from Libreville in about twenty minutes, which allows a weekend without long trips.
From November to March around, ecoguides supervise night outings to watch the turtle spawning, without any guarantee of encounter.
The rules are strict (no light, no contact, a distance to take) and a weekend costs from 60,000 to 95,000 FCFA per person, according to our estimates.

seo.description: Crossing, accommodation, night outings to see the turtles, rules and budget: the weekend guide to Pointe-Denis.

body.text: Saturday, eight o'clock. On the Libreville quay, the last bags pass from hand to hand and the boat deviates from the edge. The city is retreating: towers, cranes, concrete facade. Opposite, a green, low and continuous line. Twenty minutes later, the boat docks in front of Pointe-Denis beach. The passengers descend, bag to the shoulder, and look up at the trees. No traffic jam, no horns, only the sound of the waves. For the inhabitants of the capital, it is a quick change of scenery, and simple to organize.

The crossing is the first asset of the destination. Several operators link Libreville to Pointe-Denis in about twenty minutes, depending on the sea. The schedules depend on the tide and the weather: it is better to book the day before, especially on weekends, and confirm the time of return before leaving. Count around 20,000 FCFA per person, according to our estimates, more for a private boat. Bring a garment against the spray, and protect your devices. On the way back, keep a margin before a flight or an appointment: the sea does not always follow the schedule.
Where to sleep, where to eat

On the peninsula, the accommodation remains simple: wooden bungalows, family hostels, camps by the beach. Count from 30,000 to 70,000 FCFA per night in a double room, depending on comfort. Meals are most often ordered in advance, and it is better to warn of its arrival. The menu fits in a few dishes: grilled fish, cassava, plantain bananas. Places are counted. From November to March, when laying attracts visitors, the weekends fill up quickly. Take water, mosquito repellent and sun protection.
People believe that we are next to the city, so there will always be room. From November to March, this is not true. You have to book, and we repeat it on the phone.
body.attribution: Mireille Ngomo, manager of a family inn

body.text: Luth Turtle Season

Around Pointe-Denis, the Pongara National Park hosts, from around November to March, the lute turtle laying, the largest species of sea turtle. The females come out of the water at night, dig a nest in the sand, lay their eggs there and return to the sea. Night outings, supervised by eco-guides, allow you to attend in small groups. They last several hours and guarantee nothing: some evenings, no female comes. When a turtle appears, the scene is slow and silent: we hear the surf, the breath of the animal, the sand that falls. The appointment is fixed at the end of the evening, with the guide, who chooses the beach according to the observations of the day before.

We walk in the dark, without a lamp, on the sand. When a female comes out of the water, we stop, we wait, we let her. *The turtle is not there for us.* If you are lucky enough to see her, you should not give her a reason to leave without having laid.
body.attribution: Judicaël Ovono, Ecoguide

body.text: The ecoguides recall a few rules before each departure, and they are not negotiated:

items: No light: no lamp, flash, or screen on.
Stay behind the guide and keep the distance it indicates.
Never touch a turtle or hinder its passage to the sea.
speak in a low voice, without running or standing in front of the animal.
Don't leave anything on the beach: take your trash.

body.text: The budget for a weekend, per person

The weekend is in four positions. The round trip crossing costs around 20,000 FCFA per person. The double room costs from 30,000 to 70,000 FCFA per night, or 15,000 to 35,000 FCFA each. The weekend meals represent from 15,000 to 25,000 FCFA, and the supervised night out from 10,000 to 15,000 FCFA. These ranges vary according to the season and comfort, and exclude drinks and personal expenses.

body.label: Indicative budget for a weekend in La Pointe-Denis, per person, for two in the room
body.source: Approximate figure for this demonstration article

body.text: This weekend does not replace a stay in a large park, but it gives an accessible preview of it: a short drive, a beach, a night outside to watch an animal come to lay eggs. Nature does not follow any schedule. Better to leave without demanding a meeting: the weekend is already worth for the beach, the calm and the crossing. Other getaway ideas are brought together in our section [destinations](/rubrique/tourisme/destinations).

english.title: Travelling in Gabon: scarce lodges and costly domestic transport
english.dek: Few beds near the parks, expensive domestic flights and sometimes impassable tracks make infrastructure the main obstacle to tourism. A travel agency and a hospitality school explain what they need.
keyPoints: Lodges and camps close to the parks offer, according to our estimates, about 400 beds, which limits group size and attendance.
Domestic flights, few in number and expensive, and sometimes impassable tracks in the rainy season make every trip more expensive.
Agencies and hotel schools require regular rotations, readable rates and training adapted to work in the lodge.

seo.description: Reduced accommodation capacity, expensive domestic flights, difficult tracks: the brakes of tourism in Gabon and what professionals are asking for.

body.text: Cédric Ekogha redid the calculation three times. To send six travelers from Libreville to a lodge on the coast and then bring them back, you have to add plane tickets, transfer by boat, two nights full board and a guide. The total makes its customers hesitate even before they have looked at a photo of the site. Director of a receptive agency in Libreville, he knows the scene by heart: the enthusiasm of the first call, silence after the estimate. The problem is not the attraction of the parks. This is what you have to cross to reach them: counted accommodation, rare connections, tracks at the mercy of the rain.
too few beds

The first lock is hosting capacity. Around the parks, there are an estimated 400 beds about the offer of lodges and camps, divided between around thirty establishments. Most have between eight and twenty beds. A group of about fifteen people therefore occupies an entire site, and the agency must sometimes split it between two distant lodges. Several establishments close out of season, for lack of regular customers. The hotels of the big cities, designed for business trips, do not meet the demand of nature travelers, who want to sleep on the edge of the forest.

body.label: Estimated total capacity of lodges and camps near the parks
body.source: Approximate figure for this demonstration article

body.text: I can't sell a circuit of fifteen people. It would take two lodges, two transfers, two guides. At this point, it is easier to offer another destination.
body.attribution: Cédric Ekogha, director of a receptive agency in Libreville

body.text: Overpriced interior connections

The second lock is for transport. Domestic air rotations are few, and their prices reflect this narrowness: few passengers to be spread over high operating costs. A round trip on an internal connection often is around 150,000 FCFA, depending on the agencies consulted, excluding luggage and transfers. For a family of four, transport can weigh more than the stay. These explanations are partly structural; They nevertheless weigh on the purchase decision. A modified schedule is also sufficient to upset a program set to the nearest night.

body.label: Indicative price of a round trip on an inland air link, excluding luggage and transfers
body.source: Approximate figure for this demonstration article

body.text: The ground remains. Road runways like airstrips are unevenly maintained, and the rainy season makes some stretches impassable, which forces you to postpone or cancel. The train could ease some of the demand. The Transgabonese connects Owendo to Franceville: it offers a precious axis to cross the country, but it does not serve the coast, where there are several parks. To combine rail, road and canoe, the agencies themselves assemble links that do not speak to each other. The organization remains artisanal, and each link adds its hazard. To guard against, the agencies add a night's margin before the international return flights, which further increases the stay.
What the professionals ask for

Questioned separately, a incoming agency and a hotel school make close requests. The first calls for air rotations at fixed days to the reception areas, rates known well in advance and regular maintenance of the most popular tracks. The second pleads for internships in the lodge integrated into the course, and for training courses that are not limited to the hotel industry. Both draw the same conclusion: without quality reception, a good transport price is not enough; Without accessible transport, a good welcome remains invisible.

We train receptionists for city hotels. A lodge asks something else: knowing how to cook, driving a boat, speaking English, telling the place. These professions are learned *immersed*, not just in class.
body.attribution: Armelle Koumba, director of studies at a hotel school in Libreville

body.text: The school welcomes about fifty students per promotion, according to her, of which only a minority is targeting the lodges, for lack of identified opportunities. Internships would be possible if the establishments could supervise trainees all year round. This is the circle described by professionals: few beds, therefore few visitors; Few visitors, so few jobs trained. Gabonese nature tourism expects less of a spectacular project than a series of reliable links. To see what these sites offer once there, go to our section [National parks](/rubrique/tourisme/parcs-nationaux).

english.title: Mvet: a new generation carries on the Fang epic tradition
english.dek: In Libreville and Woleu-Ntem workshops, young musicians learn the zither used in Fang epic storytelling from their elders. Some combine it with contemporary music. How to record a tradition passed down orally remains an open question.
keyPoints: The Mvet, a zither on stem with resonance calabashes, accompanies the Fang epics, a tradition shared with Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea.
Workshops in Libreville and Oyem, in the Woleu-Ntem, organize the transmission from master to student to a young audience.
Some musicians mix the MVET with current music, while the recording of stories remains an open project.

seo.description: Workshops in Libreville and in Woleu-Ntem, young players, interbreeding with current music: the next generation of Mvet, instrument of Fang epics.

body.text: Saturday afternoon, in a room lent by a cultural center in Libreville, a teenager reaches out to the strings of a mvet. He hesitates. Facing him, Nadège Mintsa, who has been playing the instrument since childhood, takes her fingers and guides them on the strings. The sound that comes out is dry, woody, prolonged by the calabashes. Around them, a dozen students, from ten to twenty-five years old, listen without speaking. They came to learn what many of their parents only heard on the radio: the singing of epics.

The Mvet is a zither on a rod, with resonance calabashes. He accompanies the Fang epics, recited and sung by a bard called the "Bomm-Mvet". This tradition is shared with Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea. The long story is transmitted orally: it speaks of heroes, fights and wisdom, and each bard adds its voice, its way, its comments. For a long time, we became Mbom-Mvet with a master, over the years, without notebooks or diplomas. Today, this filiation is reinvented in workshops, on weekends.
From teacher to student

The Libreville workshop has existed for two years. It is led by the MVET Demain association, which holds a second in Oyem, capital of Woleu-Ntem, province of the north of the country, border with Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea. The principle is simple: a teacher, a few students, sessions on weekends. We first learn to tune the instrument, then to hold a rhythm, finally to tell. Each session begins with a listening time: the master plays, the students are silent, then each takes the sentence in turn. The elders find a listening that the city rarely grants them. In Oyem, several masters come from neighboring villages one weekend per month to teach.

body.label: apprentices welcomed each year in the workshops of Libreville and Oyem

body.text: You don't sit in front of an MVET like in front of a guitar. We first need *Shut up and listen* the master. The notes come later. Whoever wants to go too fast does not learn the story, he only learns the noise.
body.attribution: Nadège Mintsa, MVET player and workshop facilitator

body.text: When the MVET meets current music

Some young people do not stick to the old repertoire. Aymeric Edzang, 24, plays guitar in a group from Libreville. He introduced an MVET into the group, supported by a bass and percussion. The result is neither a reconstruction nor a fantasy: the sentences of the story remain, but the tempo accelerates, and choruses in French rub shoulders with the passages in Fang. Some purists frown. Others see in these crossbreeds the best chance of making the instrument hear the instrument who no longer frequent the vigils.
My grandfather would have made me start again ten times. But if he heard me play with my friends, I think he would recognize the sentences. The important thing is that we continue to sing them.
body.attribution: Aymeric Edzang, guitarist and student of the workshop

body.text: Record without freezing

The most delicate question is that of recording. The stories are long and are transmitted by word of mouth: when a master disappears, a part of the repertoire disappears with him. The association began to record vigils, with the agreement of the masters, and to transcribe certain passages. The masters set their conditions: to be present during the proofreading, to validate each transcription, to refuse any commercial distribution without their agreement. It remains to decide who keeps these archives, how we share them and under what conditions. The elders fear that a recording will freeze an art that lives on variations; Young people see it as a way to lose nothing. Both positions agree on one point: an audio file does not replace learning.

body.label: stories recorded with the agreement of the masters since the launch of the program

body.text: For the moment, the construction site is progressing to the rhythm of the availability of each other. The workshop of Libreville is looking for a larger room, that of Oyem a second instrument. The association would also like to invite players from Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea, to compare the ways of saying the same story. At the end of the session, the teenager from the beginning returns the MVET to Nadège Mintsa, fingers flushed. He asks when the next lesson will resume. More articles on Gabonese creation in our section [Music](/rubrique/culture/musique).

patrimoine-inventaire-collections-musees.dek: Restaurateurs et étudiants photographient, mesurent et décrivent masques, parures et instruments, en lien avec les musées. L'objectif : un catalogue consultable, et des collections mieux protégées de l'humidité.

english.authorBio: She investigates school, health and daily life, and recounts the Gabonese cultural scene, from museums to the studios of Libreville.
english.title: Heritage: an inventory brings museum collections into view
english.dek: Conservators and students are working with museums to photograph, measure and describe masks, ornaments and instruments. They aim to create a searchable catalogue and protect the collections from damp.
keyPoints: An association of restaurateurs and students photographs and describes masks, ornaments and instruments, in connection with museums, including the National Museum.
The equatorial climate, hot and humid, threatens wood, fibers and metals: preventive conservation becomes a priority.
The collective wants to digitize the files and open an online catalog, so that the public and researchers can consult the objects.

seo.description: Photographing, describing, digitizing: a collective of restaurateurs and students draws up an inventory of objects kept in Gabonese museums.

body.text: In front of a window of the National Museum, in Libreville, a student puts on a pair of gloves. She puts a metal bracelet on a gray background, places a graduated ruler next to it, adjusts the lighting. One click, then another: face, profile, detail of the engraved decor. At the next table, a friend notes the dimensions, the material, the condition of the surface. The pace is slow: about fifteen minutes per piece, more for a fragile object. In the room, a few visitors stop, intrigued by this meticulous work which has nothing to do with an exhibition. However, this is the beginning of a long-term project: to give each object a sheet, a photograph and a number.

The operation is led by the collective Inventory Open, an association of restaurateurs, students and volunteers. It takes place in conjunction with the museums, including the National Museum, partner of the project. The sessions take place on weekends and during the university holidays, with shooting equipment loaned by the members. Masks, ornaments, musical instruments: each piece receives the same sheet, filled with several hands and composed of five elements:

items: Photographs from multiple angles, with scale and neutral background
Dimensions and materials
state of conservation
Inventory number
known or supposed origin, with the source of the information

body.label: pieces photographed and described since the launch of the inventory

body.text: A climate that works against objects

Gabon has an equatorial, hot and humid climate. For collections, it is a permanent test. The wood deforms and attracts insects that feed on it. Fibers, leathers and textiles are moldy. Alloys are covered with corrosion products. The restaurateurs talk about preventive preservation: measuring humidity, ventilating, protecting rooms in suitable boxes, regularly checking their condition. Nothing spectacular, but these gestures are better than expensive restoration after damage. It is still necessary to know what one possesses, object by object, and in what state it is: this is precisely what the inventory allows.

In this climate, an object that we do not look at is an object that degrades. The inventory forces us to look, to compare from one visit to another, and to spot the beginning of a mold or crack in time.
body.attribution: Élodie Mouanga, restaurateur, coordinator of the collective

body.text: Know where each room comes from

As in many museums around the world, the origin of certain pieces is poorly documented: village of origin, date of manufacture, use, sometimes the community that produced it. Old registers are incomplete, labels peel off. A bracelet may have changed hands several times before entering a collection. The collective crosses the information available and collects, when possible, testimonies from alumni or craftsmen who recognize a style, a gesture, a decor. It's about adding elements, never inventing them. Each sheet therefore indicates three things: what is established, what is supposed, what remains unknown.

A mask whose provenance is unknown is a half-silent mask. He remains beautiful, but he no longer says who sculpted him, for whom, for what use. Documenting is *give him the floor* without making him say what he does not say.
body.attribution: Constant Mombo, art historian at the University

body.text: Scan, open to the public

The next step is scanning. Photographs and files feed a database that the collective wants to open online, with good quality images and texts in French, then, eventually, in national languages. The public could discover objects that the rooms cannot always show, and the schools use them to prepare their visits. A first version, limited to a few hundred cards, could open as a test. The constraints are concrete: secure storage of files, conditions of use of images, Internet access outside the capital. The officials of the collective recall that digital completes the exhibition halls without replacing them: we do not feel a mask on a screen.

The collective hopes to complete a first series in eighteen months, then extend the operation to other collections, public or private. He is looking for funding, shooting material and especially volunteers. In the meantime, each session adds some sheets to the catalog. Find our reports on the memory of the country in the section [Heritage](/rubrique/culture/patrimoine).
