english.title: Oil assets: what changes when the state takes a stake in Ozouri Petroleum
english.dek: Ivindo Capital, a public-private consortium, is taking a 40% stake in Ozouri Petroleum and its mature fields. We examine what the deal reveals about state revenue, local contractors and corporate governance.
keyPoints: A consortium involving the State and regional private investors is gaining a foothold in the Gabonese upstream.
The operation must provide additional tax revenue, without certainty on the pace of payments.
Local subcontractors are calling for written commitments on future contract volumes.

seo.description: Redemption of Ozouri Petroleum assets by Ivindo Capital: expected effects on government revenue, subcontractors and governance.

body.text: The Gabonese government enters the capital of Ozouri Petroleum. A public-private consortium called Ivindo Capital signed, on Tuesday, an agreement on the purchase of 40% of the shares of this independent oil operator, present in Gabon since 2015 on several mature fields in the coastal sedimentary basin, between Port-Gentil and Gamba. The agreement puts an end to several months of discreet negotiations, which began after the announcement of a project for a partial sale by the company's historic shareholder.

The operation values the whole of Ozouri Petroleum at around 450 billion FCFA, current dividends included, and remains subject to the agreement of the Competition Authority as well as that of the administration in charge of hydrocarbons. The schedule is not neutral: the rise in barrel prices for a year has given the appeal to mature oil assets that some investors judged, two years ago, at the end of the cycle.
A unique consortium

Ivindo Capital brings together the Gabonese state, the majority shareholder of the vehicle up to 60%, and Ogooué Ressources, a regional investment fund already present in port logistics and infrastructure financing. The two partners had already worked together on the financing of a container terminal, which facilitated the legal assembly of this more complex operation. This architecture should allow the State to influence the strategic decisions of the future together without taking on operational responsibility alone, nor the full financial risk.

body.label: Amount of IVINDO Capital's stake in Ozouri Petroleum

body.text: Ozouri Petroleum today extracts nearly 25,000 barrels per day, or about one-eighth of domestic production. Its fields, exploited for more than twenty years by various successive operators, are entering a phase of natural decline that techniques of assisted recovery, injection of water and additional boreholes, could extend from ten to fifteen years. The company directly employs nearly 400 employees, to which are added the workforce of subcontractors present on the platforms and rear bases of Port-Gentil.
What it changes for the state

For public finances, the entry into the capital gives rise to a share of the dividends, in addition to the royalties already collected on each barrel extracted, regardless of the operator's shareholding. However, the net gain remains difficult to quantify at this stage: it will depend on the price of the barrel, the pace of the payments decided by the new board of directors, and the investments that Ivindo Capital will itself have to make to extend the life of the fields.

We don't just buy barrels, we buy *A place at the table* where the investments of the next ten years are decided. It is a change of posture for the state, which becomes part of a stakeholder rather than a simple royalty collector.
body.attribution: Thierry Bouka, Managing Director of Ivindo Capital

body.text: On the subcontractor side, the announcement is welcomed with cautious optimism. About thirty Gabonese companies, from industrial maintenance to the transport of offshore personnel, depend directly on Ozouri Petroleum contracts, for cumulative amounts estimated at several tens of billions of FCFA per year. Many fear that a change in shareholding will be accompanied by a downward renegotiation in their current contracts. Ivindo Capital presented four commitments to them, during a meeting organized last week with the professional federations concerned:

items: Maintenance of maintenance contracts already awarded to local companies
Strengthening the local content clause in future calls for tenders
Opening of a training program for Gabonese technicians
Annual publication of the list of main contracts awarded to Gabonese companies

body.text: A management risk to monitor

There remains a risk that several analysts underline: the presence of the State in the capital of an operator does not, on its own, guarantee better management. Elsewhere on the continent, public equity investments in the upstream oil have sometimes weighed on the governance of the companies concerned more than they have strengthened government revenues, in particular when appointments to management positions prevailed over technical skills. IVINDO Capital claims to want to stick to a shareholder role, without intervening in the daily operational management of the fields.

The state must behave as a shareholder, not as a manager. The temptation to weigh on operational arbitrations, purchases or recruitments, is the main risk of this type of assembly. It is generally paid for by a loss of industrial efficiency.
body.attribution: Léa Nzoghe, economist specializing in extractive industries

body.text: The file was sent to the Competition Authority last week, for an examination whose regulatory duration may not exceed two months. Both parties aim to close the transaction before the end of the calendar year, subject to the regulatory timetable and obtaining the additional financing necessary for the announced investment program.

Other independent operators, faced with the same aging of their fields, will closely follow the outcome of this file: it could serve as a model, or as a foil, for the next discussions between the State and the private oil sector. In a country where oil still weighs almost 40% of GDP, the way the state chooses to intervene in the capital of operators is never a purely financial subject. Other files of the same type are brought together in our section [Mines & Energy](/rubrique/economie/mines-energie).

english.title: After oil: investigating Gabon’s three routes to diversification
english.dek: Oil still funds a third of the state budget. Timber processing, agribusiness and digital services are being promoted as engines of growth. We examine the constraints each sector faces.
keyPoints: Processed wood comes up against energy and transport costs that are still poorly controlled.
The agro-industry promises to reduce the food bill, but comes up against land and volumes.
Digital services depend on reliable electricity, available especially around Libreville.

seo.description: Processed wood, agro-industry, digital services: investigation of the three pillars supposed to relay oil in the Gabonese economy.

body.text: Oil still finances nearly a third of the Gabonese state budget. This old dependency becomes a central subject again as mature fields produce less and world prices remain unstable. The public authorities have been repeating for years the objective of a diversified economy, capable of taking an oil shock without the entire budget wavering, in a country whose gross domestic product is around 12,000 billion FCFA for approximately 2.4 million inhabitants. Three sectors are today presented as the most credible relays for this transition: processed wood, agribusiness and digital services. It is still necessary to verify what these three pillars really carry, beyond the intention displayed in the official speeches. This file examines, sector by sector, what is part of the solid plan and what remains, for the moment, of the order of the promise.

body.label: Estimated share of oil revenue in public revenue

body.text: On paper, ambition is not new. It resulted in successive stages: ban on exporting unprocessed logs in the early 2010s, tax incentives for agribusiness over the following decade, then, more recently, a proactive policy for digital services and office jobs. [Our public finance analyzes](/rubrique/economie/finances-publiques) Moreover, show to what extent the cash flow of companies remains sensitive to oil cycles, long after the raw material has left the country. Diversification is therefore not a soul supplement reserved for end-of-year speeches: it directly conditions the country's ability to cushion the next shock, regardless of its arrival date. Each of these stages has also aroused its share of skepticism, before bearing fruit more slowly than its promoters expected.

items: Processed wood: Switch from exported raw log to finished furniture and plywood on site.
Agro-industry: Reduce the food import bill through local food and cash production.
Services and digital: build an office, data and skills economy, independent of the basement.

body.text: The bet of processed wood

The wood sector remains the oldest of the three. Since the ban on exporting unprocessed logs, sawmills and unrolling units have multiplied on the outskirts of Libreville and along the axes leading to the ports. Okoumé Industries operates a plywood unit there that employs several hundred employees and targets the European and North African markets for its panels. The company claims to have doubled its production capacity in five years, driven by external demand for certified tropical wood. Competition remains strong against producers in Southeast Asia, whose freight to Europe costs less, which pushes Gabonese processors to position themselves on rarer and better valued species rather than on standardized large volumes.
We are no longer log exporters. We sell *of the finished panel*, with a brand and after-sales service.
body.attribution: Thierry Bouka, Managing Director of Okoumé Industries

body.text: the equation remains fragile. The cost of industrial energy weighs on the competitiveness of sawmills, as does road transport to export ports. Qualified labor — machine operators, maintenance technicians — still lack, and the sector imports part of its technical supervision from abroad. Industry manufacturers recognize that an electric shock or an increase in freight would be enough to cut already narrow margins. Several processors also mention the difficulty of obtaining long-term bank financing, with local banks favoring shorter deadlines than those required by a heavy industrial tool.
Agro-industry is looking for its volumes

Gabon imports most of what it consumes on a daily basis: rice, oil, poultry, some of the fresh vegetables sold in urban markets. Agribusiness is supposed to reverse this trend, year after year. Ivindo Agro-Industries has grown several thousand hectares of oil palm and cassava in the province of Ogooué, with the declared ambition to significantly reduce food imports from the country by the end of the decade. The company employs a large seasonal workforce, recruited from the neighboring villages of its plantations. Other operators, of more modest size, rely rather on peri-urban market gardening to directly supply the markets of Libreville, with shorter production cycles than those of the oil palm.

body.caption: A food plantation on the rural periphery. Agro-industry relies on cash crops and food.

body.label: Estimated share of food consumed covered by imports
body.source: Approximate figure for this demonstration article

body.text: The announced volumes come up against known obstacles: poorly readable land tenure, competition for water and rural roads, cost of transport between production areas and urban markets. Smallholders also fear being marginalized by the arrival of large concessions, for lack of sufficient support to integrate the same supply chains and the same distribution channels. Access to Crédit Agricole remains, from their point of view, a comparable obstacle: most banks still classify agro-industry among high-risk sectors, for lack of sufficient repayment history.
The bet of digital services

The third pillar is not seen from the road: these are offices, call centers, financial services and digital platforms. Digital estuary, a young IT services company based in Libreville, trains developers and exports programming services to several countries in the sub-region. Mobile payment is also progressing, carried by a young and increasingly connected clientele, to the point of competing with traditional banking counters for day-to-day transactions. Several private incubators are now accompanying young tech companies, with uneven success: some are struggling to find customers beyond a still narrow domestic market.

body.caption: an auxiliary solar installation. The rise of digital technology depends first on continuously available electricity.

body.text: This economy of services presupposes reliable electricity and a stable connection, two conditions still unequally met outside the capital. Akanda Energy, operator of an auxiliary solar power plant, feeds part of the needs of the data centers of the place, but shedding remains frequent in secondary cities. The digital sector is also gaining ground on a pool of skills that is still limited, which fuels salary competition between local employers and pushes some young graduates to try their luck abroad.
Three sectors will not replace oil in a decade. They can, if the execution follows, reduce the share of the shock that the economy takes with each fall in prices.
body.attribution: Lea Nzoghe, economist

body.text: The three pillars share the same weak point: they require time and patient capital, two rare resources in an annual budget cycle. They also share a more encouraging common point, that of not relying on a single world course to exist. Finally, they share a more discreet risk: that of being announced with more emphasis than really committed budgetary means.

None of the three pillars will be enough alone. Taken together, over a decade rather than a mandate, they draw a plausible trajectory rather than a martingale. This is also, more prosaically, what the next budgets will measure: the share of off-oil in state revenue.

seo.description: Mineral terminal and railway: how a financing of 1,200 billion FCFA should double Gabonese exports of manganese.

body.text: Funding of 1,200 billion FCFA should make it possible to double the evacuation capacity of Gabonese manganese within three years. The envelope, completed this week after several months of discussions between shareholders, combines regional bank loans, financing of export agencies and equity contribution, in a context of manganese prices that have remained high over the last two years.

It is divided into two parts: 700 billion FCFA for a new ore terminal at the port of Owendo, and 500 billion FCFA for the strengthening of the railway line that connects the mines from Haut-Ogooué to the coast, near 650 kilometers. The two projects must move forward in parallel, otherwise one will see one neutralize the capacity gains of the other.
A brand new terminal

The future terminal, entrusted to Estuaire Logistique, will double the length of the dock available and will increase the draft to 14 meters, enough to accommodate larger bulk carriers and reduce the number of rotations necessary for the same tonnage exported. The work should start in the first quarter and spread over about three years, without interruption of the existing port activity.

body.label: annual evacuation capacity referred to in Owendo, compared to 6 million tonnes today

body.text: The railway, critical link

Upstream, the railway remains the main bottleneck of the system: some single-track sections limit the number of daily convoys, and the fleet of wagons struggles to keep pace with the production rate of the mines, especially during the rainy season. The reinforcement envisages new sidings, the rehabilitation of several bridges and the purchase of additional wagons from regional suppliers.
Without this railroad upgrade, the new terminal would turn half its capacity. The two projects voluntarily advance hand in hand, piloted by the same project team.
body.attribution: Hervé Mabicka, Logistics Director of Logistics Estuary

body.text: Haut-Ogooué Manganese, which operates the main deposits concerned, highlights the local benefits of the site: Gabonese civil engineering companies associated with earthworks, subcontracting and site restoration, and opening of several positions at locally trained engineers. The Company publishes, for the first time, a detailed schedule of these commitments:

items: About 900 direct jobs over the duration of the work, according to the companies concerned
A subcontracting quota reserved for Gabonese SMEs for civil engineering
An open rail trade training program in the province
A monitoring committee involving local authorities and representatives of local residents

body.text: The rise in power of the terminal and the railway line is based on the entry into service of new mines in the Haut-Ogooué. For the State, the stakes are direct: the mining royalties are based on the tonnages actually exported, and not on the only production extracted. As long as the logistic neck persists, part of the resource remains, in fact, without immediate tax value. The next activity reports from Haut-Ogooué Manganese will therefore be followed closely, beyond the production figures alone.

english.dek: Libreville’s one-stop business registration service reports an average wait of 72 hours, down from three weeks. Opening a bank account and securing land still need to be made easier.
keyPoints: The one-stop shop groups together seven formalities in a single file and reduces business creation to 72 hours on average.
Professional bank account and land title remain the main blocking points once the company has been registered.
More than 3,200 companies have been registered since the opening of the device, before its planned extension to two other cities.

seo.description: Business creation in Libreville: The one-stop shop promises 72 hours, but bank and land account remain obstacles.

body.text: Creating a business in Libreville took, a year ago, almost three weeks and a dozen trips between different administrations, often located at the other end of the city. Some creators gave up purely and simply, or postponed their project for several months. The one-stop business start-up window announces today an average time to **72 hours** For a complete file, supporting documents included.

The principle: an entrepreneur submits a single file, in one place, and the counter takes care internally of registration in the trade register, the allocation of the tax identifier, affiliation to the social security fund and the legal publication of the creation. The entrepreneur no longer has to produce the intermediate certificates himself from one administration to another.
Seven steps, one file

Previously, these formalities implied seven distinct steps, divided between several administrative buildings, each with its opening hours, its dedicated counters and its documents to be provided, sometimes redundant from one administration to another. An incomplete file in one of them could lengthen the entire course by several weeks, the time to resume the next queue.

body.label: Average time announced for a complete file, compared to three weeks before the reform

items: Before: seven counters, about three weeks, about ten trips
After: a single file, 72 hours on average, a single drop-off point
Still outside the device: professional bank account and land title

body.text: What remains to be improved

The legal creation of the company is only one step among others. The opening of a professional bank account still takes, according to several testimonies collected from young entrepreneurs, one to two more weeks, the time that the bank instructs its own client knowledge file. Obtaining a land title for commercial premises remains the most often quoted black point, some files remaining pending for several months.
In 72 hours, I had my registration number, which surprised me a lot. I then had to wait twelve more days to open an account in the name of the company, while the bank checked my file.
body.attribution: Sandrine Okomo, founder of Nzé Design

body.text: Since the opening of the one-stop shop at the start of the year, more than 3,200 companies have been registered there, compared to just over 2,000 over the same period last year, all circuits combined. Some of these creations correspond to activities already carried out in an informal way, of which the managers took advantage of the simplification to put themselves in order. The counter does not yet communicate sectoral details, but trade and services represent, by the admission of its agents, the majority of the files processed.

The device must be extended to Port-Gentil and Franceville by the end of the year, with a stated objective: to eventually reduce all formalities to a single digital file, which can be consulted online. Other comparable initiatives are listed in our section [firms](/rubrique/economie/entreprises), where several entrepreneurs recount their own administrative journey.

english.title: Gabon opens its first Tier III-certified data centre
english.dek: Gabon’s first Tier III-certified data centre, in Akanda, promises shorter response times for local businesses. The operator is already monitoring the electricity it consumes.
keyPoints: The country has a Tier III certified data center, an alternative to hosting abroad for large Gabonese accounts.
Data repatriation greatly reduces response times, but power consumption remains a point of vigilance.
Banks, telecom operators and administrations are the first targeted customers, driven by the local data retention requirement.

seo.description: Tier III data center in Akanda: reduced latency for Gabonese companies, but electricity consumption remains a challenge.

body.text: Gabon now has a Tier III certified data center, a first in the country. The infrastructure, installed in Akanda, at the exit of Libreville, was put into service this month by the digital estuary operator, after eighteen months of work carried out in part by local electrical engineering companies. The site also has direct access to two separate optical fiber loops, a condition set by several customers before signing their contract.

The Tier III certification, an internationally recognized industry standard, imposes a redundancy in critical equipment: power supply, air conditioning and connectivity can fail in isolation without interrupting service to hosted customers, with an announced availability close to 99.98% over one year full.
The end of remote accommodation

So far, a large part of the data of Gabonese companies and administrations has passed through servers located in Europe, due to a lack of local infrastructure that meets the security standards required by large bank and industrial accounts. This choice has a direct cost, billed in foreign currency, and a significant latency time for the end user connected from Libreville or inside the country.

items: Banking applications requiring a very short response time
Health databases subject to strict privacy rules
sites and public services consulted mainly from the national territory

body.label: Response time for a user logged in from Libreville, before and after an application repatriates, depending on the operator

body.text: An electric bill to monitor

A data center of this size consumes continuously: the installed power reaches 8 megawatts, with a payload objective around 6 megawatts once the first rooms are filled, i.e. the consumption of a district of around 15,000 households. The power supply combines public grid and standby generators, sized to last for several days in the event of a prolonged break.

Electrical availability is our first topic of vigilance, even before computer security. A data center does not forgive the cuts, and our customers contractually demand it in the service levels we guarantee them.
body.attribution: Fabrice Ogandaga, Technical Director of Digital Estuary

body.text: The operator primarily targets banks, telecommunications operators and administrations subject to data retention obligations on the national territory. The argument of digital sovereignty weighs more and more in public tenders, as IT security incidents multiply on a regional scale, including among several neighbors in the CEMAC sub-region.

A second room, twice as large, is already under consideration. It will partly depend on the ability of the local electrical network to absorb an additional load without weakening the surrounding neighborhoods, an arbitration that will necessarily involve the national electricity network manager in the next stages of the project.

english.title: Gabon’s coast: an economic lifeline under pressure
english.dek: Along more than 800 kilometres of coast, Gabon’s economic activity brings competing pressures. Erosion, industrial and artisanal fishing, waterfront development and port expansion all vie for space.
keyPoints: Artisanal fishing and industrial fishing are disputed with poorly controlled coastal areas.
Real estate pressure reduces public access to the seaside in urban areas.
The extension of the harbor changes the currents and moves some traditional fishing areas.

seo.description: Erosion, artisanal fishing against industrial fishing, land pressure, port extension: investigation into Gabonese coastline tensions.

body.text: Over nearly eight hundred kilometers, the Gabonese coast concentrates most of the country's economic activity: the capital, the first oil port, the main logistics bases. This facade is also the most exposed. Erosion, urbanization of the seaside and competition for the space between fishermen, promoters and port authorities redraw, year after year, a coastline that was believed to be stable.

body.label: Gabonese coastal length exposed to coastal erosion
body.source: Approximate figure for this demonstration article

body.text: Two peaches for the same lagoon

Artisanal fishing, practiced from motorized canoes, supports tens of thousands of families along the coast. It cohabits, sometimes badly, with industrial ships which target the same species further offshore. Artisanal fishermen denounce poorly respected exclusive fishing areas; Industrial shipowners recall that they employ local crews and supply most of the volumes exported to regional markets.
Our canoes cannot follow the trawlers off. When they fish too close to the coast, these are *Our empty return nets*.
body.attribution: Étienne Mavoungou, president of a cooperative of artisanal fishermen

body.text: Fishing manufacturers refer to their economic weight: Atlantique Pêche Gabon claims several hundred direct jobs and a significant part of the country's fisheries exports. The coexistence of the two fisheries implies, according to the administrations concerned, a better control of the areas reserved for artisanal fishing, more than a brutal arbitration in favor of one or the other.
The land by the sea

In the city, the seaside attracts hotel and residential developers, who buy or negotiate plots formerly occupied by fishing districts or undeveloped public land. This land pressure gradually changes the face of the urban coast: less direct public access to the beach, more private enclosures and closed residences.

Erosion further complicates the equation. Several coastal districts had to deal with the retreat of the coastline, which weakens the foundations built too close to the water and pushes some residents to ask for dykes or riprap, sometimes financed by the public power, sometimes by the local residents themselves.

The port, for its part, continues its extension. Logistics estuary, which operates several terminals, has dredged new channels to accommodate deeper ships. These works locally modify the currents and, according to local fishermen, distance certain schools of fish from traditional coastal fishing areas.

None of these files - fishing, land, erosion, port - can be treated in isolation: they are played on the same coastline, with actors who have neither the same time horizon nor the same balance of power. The coast will remain, for the Gabonese economy, a valuable and increasingly disputed asset.

english.title: Solar power: 120 MW planned for Owendo and Port-Gentil
english.dek: Two solar plants with a combined capacity of 120 MW are due to supply Owendo and Port-Gentil by 2027. They would diversify the power supply, with grid connection still a major undertaking.
keyPoints: Two consortia, Akanda Energy and Ogooué Solar, won the tender for two 70 and 50 megawatt solar power plants.
The negotiated purchase price, about 68 FCFA per kilowatt hour, would be lower than that of the auxiliary thermal power plants used at the peak.
Connecting the two sites to the existing network requires reinforcements, the full funding of which is not yet completed.

seo.description: Two 120 megawatt solar power plants must power Owendo and Port-Gentil, with an expected effect on costs, but still uncertain connection.

body.text: Two photovoltaic power plants, totaling 120 megawatts, are to be created near Owendo and Port-Gentil by 2027. The Gabonese authorities have awarded the two projects following an international call for tenders launched In 2022, to which a dozen consortia had responded. The initial schedule provided for an allocation a year earlier, delayed by several administrative appeals.

Gabonese electricity today largely depends on hydroelectricity, supplemented by thermal power plants mobilized during peak or low water periods, when the flow of rivers falls. Solar remains, for the moment, marginal in this mix, with a handful of small installations already in service. A few public administration roofs are already hosting panels, but on a scale that is unparalleled with the two projects announced.
Diversify the electric mix

In Owendo, the consortium **Akanda Energy** Must build a 70 megawatt plant on land near the industrial zone. In Port-Gentil, Ogooué Solaire is loaded with a 50 megawatt installation, designed to support the local network during peak consumption. The commissioning of the two sites is announced for 2027. The two sites will occupy several tens of hectares each, on land already identified by the local authorities.
“These two plants will not replace hydroelectricity, they relieve it when the rivers drop. »
body.attribution: Carine Obame, Managing Director of Akanda Energy

body.label: Purchase price negotiated per kilowatt hour, compared to more than 90 FCFA for thermal appoint

body.text: An expected effect on costs

The industrialists installed around Owendo, the country's leading electricity consumers with the port areas, are hoping for a light bill at times when solar is running at full speed. Some mention a share of the solar power of up to 4% of the national electric mix by 2028. However, nothing is guaranteed before the effective commissioning of the two power plants. Current industrial tariffs vary significantly across areas and consumption levels, which complicates any uniform numerical promise.

The two consortia still have to finalize the financing of the storage equipment necessary to smooth production in the event of persistent clouds. This component, less publicized than the announced power, partly determines the real reliability of the two power stations. Without sufficient storage, production falls at sunset, at the very moment when part of the industrial demand remains high.

The connection of the two plants to the existing network remains the most uncertain point of the project. The current lines must be reinforced to absorb intermittent production, without the financing of this work being fully completed, according to the two project leaders. No specific schedule for strengthening the network has so far been made public.
“We know how to build a plant. The hardest part is often the last mile of cable. »
body.attribution: Carine Obame

body.text: The commissioning remains conditional on the progress of these connection works. The two consortia ensure that they will keep the 2027 calendar, without removing all the uncertainties that weigh on the existing infrastructure, nor on the pace of disbursements expected from donors. From now to commissioning, the Gabonese electric mix will continue to be based, as today, on hydroelectricity and thermal make-up.

nouveau-code-investissements-six-changem.dek: Seuils d’agrément relevés, avantages fiscaux resserrés, contenu local renforcé : le texte redessine les règles du jeu pour les investisseurs installés au Gabon, avec plusieurs points encore en suspens.

english.title: New investment code: six changes investors should know about
english.dek: Higher approval thresholds, tighter tax incentives and stronger local-content rules change the terms for investors operating in Gabon. Several details are still pending.
keyPoints: The special regime is no longer accessible to small projects: the minimum investment thresholds have been raised by sector.
The tax exemptions are now decreasing and limited in time, against an identical fixed term before.
A one-stop shop with expanded skills and a better-marked recourse must shorten the deadlines for examining files.

seo.title: Investment Code: The Six Changes
seo.description: Accreditation thresholds, taxation, local content, one-stop shop, recourse, safeguard clause: what the new investment code changes.

body.text: The new investment code came into force this month, after several years of discussions between the administration and the employers' organizations. The text replaces a device deemed too uniform by a more selective regime, designed to direct capital towards sectors deemed priorities and limit the windfall effects observed under the Ancien Régime. Six developments concentrate most of the practical changes for companies already established as well as for project leaders who are preparing an accreditation file. Business law professionals are already anticipating a wave of early renewal requests, the time that the actors already installed arbitrate between the two regimes.

items: Approval thresholds raised to access the special plan
Shortened and decreasing tax advantages
A stronger local content obligation in several sectors
A one-stop shop with expanded skills
a better marked right of appeal in the event of refusal
A safeguard clause that allows temporary suspension of benefits

body.text: Approval thresholds recorded

To benefit from the special scheme, a project had so far justified a modest minimum investment, which opened the system to a large number of small structures. The new text raises this floor and indexes it to the sector of activity: the threshold increases to three hundred million FCFA for services, against one hundred million previously, and to seven hundred million FCFA for industry and mines. Small structures, particularly in services, are in fact oriented towards the common law regime, which are less advantageous but also less restrictive in terms of supporting documents and administrative follow-up.
tight tax advantages

Corporate tax exemption is no longer granted for a fixed term identical to all projects, regardless of their sector or profitability. It becomes degressive: full rate in the first years, then gradual reduction until the complete extinction of the advantage. The objective stated by the administration is to avoid the windfall effects observed on already profitable projects, which continued to benefit from a total exemption several years after their start, without the tax advantage no longer conditional on any investment decision.
Strengthened local content

The share of goods and services that the investor must obtain from suppliers based in Gabon becomes a condition for maintaining the benefits granted, and no longer a simple recommendation in the establishment agreement. The rate required varies according to the sectors, with a stricter treatment for extraction and construction than for services, where the qualified local supply remains more limited. Failure to comply with this rate, observed during the annual check, can now alone justify a partial withdrawal of the advantages.

body.label: Minimum share of local subcontracting required in extraction projects, according to new text

body.text: One-stop shop and remedies

The counter in charge of the investigation of applications sees its powers expanded: it now centralizes the granting of approval, the annual monitoring of commitments made and the examination of applications for renewal, which previously fell under several separate services. In the event of refusal or withdrawal of approval, the investor has a prior administrative appeal, to be exercised within a time limit set by the text, then a contentious appeal before the competent court if he does not obtain satisfaction. This double appeal, with delays now enforceable against the administration, replaces a regime where the silence kept on a request was often worth tacit refusal, without clear deadline.
"The text is more demanding at the entrance, but more predictable in use: we finally know how soon a response must arrive"
body.attribution: Ms. Léa Nzoghe, Business Lawyer

body.text: Safeguard clause, the exception that worries

The text also introduces a safeguard clause, which allows the State to temporarily suspend certain tax advantages in the event of a serious shock on public finances. The employers' organizations consulted during the elaboration of the text fear an extensive use of this faculty, which would break the predictability also sought by the entire reform. The administration assures for its part that it would only be activated on an exceptional basis, for a limited period and after consultation with the sectors concerned, without these guarantees appearing explicitly in the body of the text. An implementing decree is announced to specify the criteria triggering this clause, without a firm schedule at this stage.
what remains blurry

Several implementing decrees, in particular on the precise calculation of the rate of local content per sector, were not yet published at the time of writing this article. The consulting firms recommend that project holders submit their file taking into account the two sets of rules, old and new, while the secondary texts are stabilized. An initial application report is promised by the administration within twelve months of entry into force. These same project leaders will follow with interest the [Public tenders](/rubrique/espace-pro/opportunites) Currently open, also concerned by the rise in local content requirements.

seo.title: Call for tenders: 14 road rehabilitation lots
seo.description: Fourteen lots of road works, six provinces, submission of files until October 30: criteria of admissibility and schedule of the call for tenders.

body.text: The Contracting Authority has published a call for tenders relating to the rehabilitation of fourteen road sections, for a cumulative length close to three hundred kilometers. The program is intended to be a priority to open up areas of agricultural and forest production, which are still poorly linked to the main commercial axes. Applications are expected until October 30, as proof of deposit, and only complete files on this date will be examined by the Commission. The optional site visits are organized on request from the technical department.
Fourteen lots, six provinces

items: Estuary: three lots, including a peri-urban section of Libreville
Woleu-Ntem: two lots linking cocoa production areas
Ngounié: three lots on the axis linking Mouila to neighboring localities
Ogooué-Maritime: two lots around Port-Gentil
Nyanga and Ogooué-Lolo: four lots spread over secondary axes

body.text: Each lot is the subject of a separate file, with a turnaround time between eight and eighteen months depending on the length of the line concerned. The amounts communicated by the contracting authority remain indicative: they are based on an administrative estimate and not on the financial offer, the only ones to set the final market price. As an indication, they range from about nine hundred million FCFA for the smallest lot to just over eight billion FCFA for the most important.
Conditions of admissibility

The application file must include a provisional guarantee equivalent to two percent of the estimated amount of the lot, references of at least two comparable road sites carried out over the past five years, as well as a certificate of financial capacity issued by a banking establishment. Groups of companies are admitted, subject to a clearly designated agent in the application form. The technical evaluation relates in particular to the earthmoving equipment available and the experience of the supervisory staff proposed for each site.

body.label: Cumulative linear of the fourteen lots put on call for tenders

body.text: "The deadlines are tenable if the payment of the start-up advance quickly follows the notification: this is often where the construction sites are falling behind, not in the field"
body.attribution: Mr. Rodrigue Essono, manager of a public works company

body.text: Procedure calendar

The withdrawal of files is open as soon as the notice is published. The submission of offers is closed on October 30 at noon. The opening bid session is public; The provisional allocation is expected within six weeks of filing, subject to the time limit for reviewing any appeals.

Candidates are invited to check the exact composition of each lot with the service in charge of withdrawing the files, the shelves that can be adjusted to the margin before closing. Bid companies also have an interest in anticipating the new local content rules, presented in our section [regulations](/rubrique/espace-pro/reglementations). A contradictory meter is planned at the start of the construction site to adjust, if necessary, the final amount of the contract.

english.title: Continuing training: what the new system means for employers
english.dek: Training contributions and the rules for funding training plans are changing. Employers, including smaller businesses, need to update their practices before the financial year ends.
keyPoints: The training contribution remains based on the payroll, but its rate now varies according to the company's workforce.
The annual training plan must be filed before the expenditure initiation, and no longer presented a posteriori.
Very small companies benefit from an increased care rate, in return for a simplified file.

seo.title: Continuing education: what changes for employers
seo.description: Training contribution, annual plan, increased support for very small companies: what changes for Gabonese employers.

body.text: The continuing education system changes logic. So far based on a minimum expenditure obligation, the employers' contribution is becoming a pooled financing tool, with a support rate that varies according to the size of the company and the nature of the training action taken. The departments responsible for examining the files announce faster processing for requests in accordance with the new standard form.
A contribution modulated according to the workforce

The training contribution rate, calculated on the gross payroll, remains generally stable for companies with more than fifty employees. On the other hand, it decreases for structures with less than ten employees, which in return benefit from simplified access to the reimbursement of their training actions, without having to justify such a detailed plan as that required of large companies. However, the latter remain required to declare each action, even modest, to remain eligible for the reduced rate.
The training plan, now prior

Another notable change: the annual training plan must now be filed before the expenses are incurred, and no longer presented a posteriori to justify a reimbursement request. Companies that do not anticipate this deposit are exposed to a refusal to support, even for training otherwise eligible and provided by an approved body. The services concerned recommend a deposit at least one month before the start of the first action provided for in the plan.

items: Submission of the annual training plan before March 31
Training agreements signed before the start of the action
Support request accompanied by invoices paid
Attestation of presence of trained employees

body.text: the case of very small businesses

Companies with less than ten employees benefit from an increased care rate, presented by the administration as an incentive for continuing education in the most fragile structures. seo.title: Central Bank Annual Report: Numbers
seo.description: Money supply, credit to the economy, foreign exchange reserves, key rate: figures from the central bank's annual report, explained.

body.text: The Zone Central Bank has published its annual report. The document draws up an inventory of the money supply, credit to the economy, foreign reserves and the orientation of monetary policy for the past financial year. Four indicators particularly hold the attention of business treasurers and financial departments, who draw benchmarks from it to build their own cash flow forecasts.
rising money supply

The money supply progresses over the year, driven by the increase in corporate sightings and by a more dynamic than anticipated urban household savings collection. This increase also reflects the growing banking of transactions, encouraged by the development of mobile payments in the main cities of the country. Retail banks confirm this trend in their own account opening statistics.

items: Money: Progress over the year
Credit to the economy: moderate growth, focused on trade
Foreign exchange reserves: coverage of several months of imports
Key rate: unchanged over the period under review

body.text: Credit to the economy, always focused

Credit to the economy is increasing at a more moderate pace than the money supply. It remains focused on trade and services, far ahead of industry and agriculture, which are struggling to mobilize medium-term financing. The banks justify this caution by the difficulty in assessing the risk over long production cycles, in the absence of sufficiently liquid guarantees for agro-industrial projects.

body.label: Share of credit to the economy oriented towards trade and services over the period under review

body.text: Foreign exchange reserves and key rate

Foreign exchange reserves cover several months of imports of goods and services, a level deemed comfortable by the analysts consulted. The key rate remains unchanged over the period, with the emission institute favoring stability as long as inflationary pressures remain contained throughout the zone. Several local economists nevertheless believe that a revision is not to be excluded if energy prices are rising again.
"The level of reserves gives margin, but it does not exempt companies from covering their currency risk on currency contracts"
body.attribution: Ms. Chantal Ivinza, economist in a local bank

body.text: For the financial departments, this annual report remains above all a calibration tool: it makes it possible to resituate the financing conditions of each company in relation to the general credit trend in the area. The next quarterly publications will make it possible to verify whether these trends are confirmed. To resituate these amounts on a national scale, Gabon's gross domestic product is around 12,000 billion FCFA, and the state budget just over 4,000 billion FCFA in the current financial year. Our other economic decryptions are brought together in the section [PRO SPACE](/rubrique/espace-pro).

editorial-diversifier-vraiment.title: Diversifier, vraiment
editorial-diversifier-vraiment.dek: Depuis quinze ans, chaque plan promet de diversifier l'économie gabonaise. Notre rédactrice en chef explique pourquoi seule la part des recettes non pétrolières permet de juger ces promesses.

english.authorBio: She directs the editorial staff of BOMA Infos. Former correspondent in Central Africa, she follows the life of institutions, public finances and public policies.
english.title: Diversification that can be measured
english.dek: For fifteen years, every plan has promised to diversify Gabon’s economy. Our editor-in-chief argues that the share of government revenue from outside the oil sector is the measure that can put those promises to the test.
keyPoints: The editorial staff defends a single credible indicator: the share of State revenue that does not come from oil or mines.
This share remains close to 42%, almost stable for ten years, despite the succession of diversification plans.
The newspaper undertakes to publish a few simple indicators each year rather than relaying new announcements.

seo.description: Editorial: The diversification of the Gabonese economy is not measured by the announced plans, but by the share of non-oil revenue.

body.text: diversify the economy. The formula has come up in all economic policy speeches for fifteen years, regardless of the government in office, regardless of the price of a barrel that day. She ended up losing her meaning by dint of being repeated without being measured, to the point of becoming a figure of speech rather than a verifiable objective.

We say it bluntly, at the risk of displeasing formulas to numbers: diversification is not decreed in a five-year plan, nor in a solemn back-to-school speech. It is measured, each year, by a single simple question. What part of the state's revenue comes from something other than oil and mines?
The counter does not move

The answer is known, and it is uncomfortable. Hydrocarbons and mines still provide just over 42% of the state's total revenue, a proportion almost unchanged for ten years, despite three full cycles of rising and falling barrel prices. The cycles vary this figure by a few points from one year to the next, but the background trend does not move.

During this time, the diversification plans followed one another, each with its acronym and its "horizon 2030", each listing, in almost the same order, the same priority sectors: agro-industry, tourism, digital economy, processed wood. There is no shortage of intentions, nor are the studies of international firms commissioned to support them. It is the results measured, year after year, that are lacking.
What our own pages say

Just read the pages that precede it. An entrepreneur who creates his company in 72 hours but waits twelve more days to open a bank account. An agricultural processing plant that takes four years to raise funding that the banks consider too risky, even though the product it manufactures is imported each year for several billion FCFA. It is these details, and not the great speeches, that decide whether a country is diversifying or just talking about them.

Even the country's first data center, presented as a step forward for digital sovereignty, comes up against a trivial question: the availability of electricity. We do not build a service economy on a network that cuts, any more than we attract foreign investors with promises that no indicator comes to corroborate.
We do not diversify an economy by decree. we diversify it *Land by land, credit by credit, kilowatt per kilowatt*. The rest is just communication.
body.attribution: Nadia Ondo

body.text: measure, not announce

What we are proposing is nothing original: tracking down, year after year, a handful of simple indicators rather than the number of plans signed or organized forums. the evolution of the non-oil share in state revenue. the number of formalized companies that survive beyond three years of existence. The volume of bank credit actually granted to the agro-industrial sector, and not the only announcements of financing lines.

This number is not dependent, and it is also not an exercise of convenience. The one-stop shop in Libreville, the first cassava starch factory, the optical fiber that reaches Franceville: these are real progress, obtained by people who have done the job rather than the speech, often with more modest means than those announced in the big plans. But their addition remains, for the moment, marginal on the scale of the State budget.

items: the share of non-oil revenue in the state budget, followed each year without exception
The three-year survival rate of newly formalized companies, sector by sector
The volume of bank credit actually granted to agro-industrial and manufacturing sectors

body.text: It will be objected that Gabon is not alone in facing this dilemma, that dependency on commodities affects most of the economies of the sub-region, and that world prices are beyond any national decision. It's true, and it doesn't change the basics: the countries that have moved their share of non-oil revenues elsewhere in the world have done so by patiently correcting their own internal obstacles, not waiting for the prices of the barrel to serve them.

None of this is settled in a budget year, or even in a legislature. Diversification is a matter of ten years, not eighteen months, and we will not write the opposite to please anyone, nor to sell more numbers.

But ten years, this is counted, year by year, figure by number. We make a commitment to publish, each year, these few indicators, whether good or bad, rather than just relaying the next plan and its procession of good intentions.
Diversification is not proclaimed. It reads in a column of digits, and this column, we will keep it open, number after number.

tribune-foret-gabonaise-credit-carbone.title: La forêt gabonaise vaut mieux qu’un crédit carbone
tribune-foret-gabonaise-credit-carbone.dek: Vendre des crédits carbone valorise la forêt au prix du renoncement. La transformer en bois d’œuvre certifié et en emplois industriels la valorise au prix du travail. Le choix n’est pas neutre.

english.authorBio: An economist by training, he animates the ideas pages and regularly signs forums. His analyzes engage only him.
english.title: Gabon’s forests are worth more than carbon credits
english.dek: Carbon credits put a value on forests by paying people to forgo using them. Certified timber and industrial jobs create value through work. The choice has consequences.
keyPoints: A carbon credit remunerates the absence of exploitation, when the second transformation of wood remunerates the work and forms a qualified workforce.
The voluntary carbon market remains illiquid and exposes the seller to high price volatility, unlike an export contract.
The two logics are not fully excluded, but one creates sustainable jobs when the other creates very little.

seo.title: Forum: The Gabonese forest is better than a carbon credit
seo.description: Forum: The Gabonese forest transformed into certified lumber and jobs is worth more than the same area sold in carbon credits.

body.text: I understand the temptation of carbon credit. A hectare of intact forest can now generate an income without a single tree being cut down, at a time when the state is looking for non-mining resources to diversify its revenue. On paper, the equation is attractive. On the ground, once the contracts have been signed and the prices negotiated, it deserves to be looked more closely.
Carbon credit argument, serious

We must recognize its consistency. The Gabonese forest stores a considerable volume of carbon; Preserving it has a real climatic value, which the voluntary market seeks precisely to monetize. For masses that are difficult to access, where logging would be marginal in any case, this remuneration can represent a net income for the municipalities concerned. Several pilot projects have thus made it possible to finance forest monitoring posts that are otherwise difficult to budget for.
What the carbon market does not say

But this market remains illiquid and its prices have seen strong variations in recent years, according to the verification scandals which have affected several projects on the continent. An income that depends on a volatile course, decided far from Gabon, exposes sellers to a risk that they do not control and that they cannot cover. An over-the-counter contract, poorly negotiated, may thus be worth much less than expected at the time of renewal.
“We signed a carbon credit agreement thinking of securing a regular income; The prize was divided by three the following year, without our recourse."
body.attribution: Ms. Estelle Bivigou, Researcher in Forest Economics

body.text: Transformation, another value scale

The second transformation of wood follows another logic. A raw exported log is worth significantly less than the same amount of wood transformed into veneer, plywood or furniture. Each transformation step adds value and, above all, use: sawyers, dryer operators, carpenters, quality controllers. A second-transformation unit installed near a exploited massif also anchors indirect jobs, from transport to industrial maintenance.

body.label: order of magnitude of the use generated by a cubic meter of wood, compared to the same volume exported in logs

body.text: I am not pleading for the abandonment of any carbon compensation: on truly marginal plots for exploitation, it retains meaning, especially when it finances verifiable community projects. But making it the main horizon of forest policy would amount to choosing rent against industry, at the precise moment when the timber sector begins to structure a certified and exportable offer.
what i remember

A forest massif transformed into certified lumber, carpentry jobs and industrial skills is, over time, more than the same surface converted into tonnes of carbon avoided. The Gabonese forest deserves better than a renunciation income. It is this industrial choice that forest policy should assume more.

interview-sans-transformation-locale-nou.title: « Sans transformation locale, nous exportons nos emplois »
interview-sans-transformation-locale-nou.dek: Présidente du Cercle des entreprises du Gabon, Sylvie NTSAME plaide pour une politique industrielle tenue dans la durée. Elle explique pourquoi, selon elle, exporter la matière première revient à exporter les emplois qui vont avec.

english.authorBio: She directs the editorial staff of BOMA Infos. Former correspondent in Central Africa, she follows the life of institutions, public finances and public policies.
english.title: ‘Without local processing, we export our jobs’
english.dek: Sylvie Ntsame, president of the Cercle des entreprises du Gabon, calls for an industrial policy that lasts. She explains why exporting raw materials also means exporting the jobs that go with them.
keyPoints: An industrial policy is judged over ten years: constancy counts more than the amount of incentives.
Exporting a raw material amounts, according to her, to exporting the uses of its processing.
The cost and reliability of energy are hampering industry as much as the technical skills gap.

seo.description: Interview with the president of the Cercle des Entreprises du Gabon on industrialization, employment and the absence of local transformation.

body.text: President of the Cercle des Entreprises du Gabon for two years, Sylvie Ntsame also runs a family-owned building materials company in Libreville. It pleads for a more restrictive industrial policy, even if it means displeasing some of its own importing members. Maintenance.
On industrial competitiveness
Employers have long demanded a more proactive industrial policy. What exactly do you expect from the public authorities?

We expect consistency. A company that invests in a processing unit commits its capital over ten or fifteen years. It needs a stable tax and customs framework over this period, not a one-year advantage and called into question the next. It is this predictability that is missing the most, even more than the amount of incentives themselves.
You use the formula "We export our jobs". What do you mean by that?

Whenever a raw material leaves the country in a raw state, most of the added value – and therefore of the skilled jobs that go with it – is created elsewhere, in the processing plants. wood, [manganese](/rubrique/economie/mines-energie), part of our agricultural production: the mechanism is the same every time. We export the material and we let go, with it, the jobs of engineers, technicians and specialized workers who could have existed here.
An industrial policy is not decreed in a Council of Ministers. It is built over ten years, *with consistency*, not ads.
body.attribution: Sylvie Ntsame, President of the Cercle des Entreprises du Gabon

body.text: Some of your members live from imports. Isn't there a conflict of interest within employers itself?

It exists, and I do not deny it. A part of our members imports finished products and has no interest in the emergence of competing local production in the short term. Our role is precisely to arbitrate between these short-term interests and the long-term collective interest, which is to have a more diversified economy and less dependent on imports.
on employment and training
Vocational training is often cited as the main obstacle to industrialization. Do you share this finding?

partly only. The lack of technical skills is real, but it does not explain everything. I have seen companies give up an industrial investment not for lack of finding technicians, but for lack of reliable electricity or landscaped land. Training is necessary, it is not sufficient.

body.label: Share of technical positions that industrialists in the sector are struggling to fill locally, according to our members

body.text: Concretely, what does the employers on training offer?

We are pushing for co-constructed learning paths with companies, where the student spends half his time in the workshop rather than on the school's only benches. Several of our members have already opened their production lines to long-term interns. This is a beginning, not yet a coherent national policy.
The cost of energy often comes up in employers' speeches. Is this really the first brake?

For heavy industry, yes, without hesitation. A processing plant that runs twenty-four hours out of twenty-four cannot deal with regular cuts or with a higher industrial tariff than that of its regional competitors. Until this equation is settled, some projects will remain on paper.
A word to conclude: can Gabon really turn into a decade?

A decade is short to change the structure of an economy, but it's enough to launch credible trajectories if you stick to it. What I fear the most is not the lack of ambition displayed, it is impatience: to want results in two years on investments that require ten.
